hook_first_line: My husband stopped wearing slippers in October because he couldn't feel them on his feet anymore.
body_full:
My husband stopped wearing slippers in October because he couldn't feel them on his feet anymore.

He didn't say that's why. He's not the kind of man who says anything. He just stopped putting them on.

I noticed because Ray has worn the same brown leather slippers for 11 years, the ones our daughter Becca bought him for Christmas back when she was still in nursing school, and he wore them every morning from the bed to the coffee pot to the back porch where he reads the paper and looks at the birds on the feeder.

Then one Tuesday in October I came out of the bathroom and he was standing in the kitchen in just his socks. White cotton socks. On the cold tile.

I said, "Where are your slippers?"

He looked down at his feet like he was surprised to see them there.

He said, "I don't know. I guess I forgot."

He didn't forget.

I want to tell you about my husband.

His name is Ray and he's 65 years old and we live in a yellow ranch house on the south side of Tulsa, Oklahoma, on a street where everybody mostly minds their own business but waves when you drive past.

Ray was an HVAC technician for 38 years. He retired at 62. He has hands like baseball gloves and a laugh like a screen door slamming. He's the most patient man I have ever known.

He's also a Type 2 diabetic, diagnosed when he was 53, which is 12 years ago now.

We've done everything. The metformin. The blood sugar log book on the kitchen counter that he updates every morning at 6:40 AM after he tests his finger. The walking. The cutting back on the foods he loves. He doesn't drink Dr. Pepper anymore and that was the hardest thing he ever gave up, harder than cigarettes, which he gave up in 1998.

For a long time he was fine. The numbers were okay. The doctor said good job, Ray, keep doing what you're doing.

Then about 3 years ago his feet started going numb.

Just a tingle at first. Pins and needles after he sat too long. He'd shake his foot out and laugh it off.

Then it was both feet. Then it was the bottoms of his feet feeling like they were wrapped in cotton. Then it was the burning at night, the kind he'd describe as "like somebody dipped my feet in vinegar." He'd kick the sheets off at 2 AM. I'd hear him out in the kitchen filling a bowl with cold water and putting his feet in it.

The doctor said it was diabetic neuropathy.

He said, "Ray, this is what happens. We manage it. We don't fix it."

That sentence has been ringing in my head for 3 years.

We manage it. We don't fix it.

The neurologist Dr. Vargas put him on gabapentin first. Took the edge off the burning a little. Made him groggy. Made him forgetful. He left the truck running in the Walmart parking lot one afternoon and didn't realize it for an hour. He was halfway home when I called him from the produce aisle wondering where he went.

Then they switched him to Lyrica. Lyrica was worse. It made his ankles swell up like grapefruits and he gained 16 pounds in 6 weeks and he stopped being able to follow the plot of a TV show.

We went back. Dr. Vargas said we could try both at lower doses. So now Ray is on two medications that don't fix anything, that just take the edge off, that make him slow and puffy and not quite himself, and his feet are still numb, and the burning still comes at 2 AM, and he sleeps in the recliner now most nights because lying flat makes it worse.

This is what we mean when we say "managing it."

This is what the system calls success.

My husband, who used to be on his feet 10 hours a day crawling through attics in 110 degree summer heat, who used to dance with me in the kitchen when George Strait came on the radio, who used to chase our grandkids around the backyard pretending to be a bear, can't feel the floor.

And his slippers sat by the bed.

In October I started to lose him.

Not all at once. Slowly. Like a radio station fading out as you drive away from town.

He stopped going out to the back porch in the morning to look at the birds. He said it was too hard to walk on the wood with bare feet. He said the floorboards felt different than they used to.

He stopped going to Lowe's on Saturday mornings. He used to spend 2 hours there walking the aisles, talking to the guys in the plumbing section, coming home with one washer and a story about somebody he ran into. He stopped going because he said it tired him out too much and his feet hurt by the time he got back to the truck.

He stopped going to church. He said his feet got cold in the pew and he didn't want to be uncomfortable for an hour.

He stopped going downstairs to his workshop. He used to be down there 4 nights a week building things. Birdhouses for the church craft fair. A jewelry box for my mother before she passed. A toy chest for our grandson Eli. He stopped because he said the stairs felt funny and he didn't trust his feet.

He just sat in the recliner.

And I sat in the kitchen pretending I wasn't watching.

I want to tell you something I haven't told anyone, including Ray.

In late October, after he'd been in that recliner for about 3 weeks straight, I went into the bedroom one afternoon while he was napping in the living room and I sat on his side of the bed and I looked at his slippers.

They were dusty. Not a lot. But enough to see.

His slippers had been dusty for 3 weeks.

And I sat there and I cried so hard my chest hurt, because I realized what it meant. It wasn't that he forgot them. It wasn't that he was being lazy. It was that he was retreating from his own life one piece at a time, and the slippers were the first thing to go, and the porch was the second, and Lowe's was the third, and his workshop was the fourth, and I didn't know what was going to be the fifth, but I knew it was coming.

I have known this man since I was 22 years old.

I was watching him disappear from inside the same body.

I called Becca that night after Ray fell asleep in the recliner.

Becca is our oldest. She's 38. She's a hospice nurse at the Saint Francis Health System in Oklahoma City. She drives down to see us about once a month. She has a son named Eli who is 6, and a husband named Curtis, who is a good man.

She works with dying people for a living and I think it has made her one of the most honest people I have ever met.

I told her about the slippers.

She was quiet for a long time on the phone.

Then she said, "Mom. I'm coming down on Friday. I want to talk to you about something."

She came down on Friday.

I made chili because that's what I make when Becca comes home. We ate at the kitchen table. Ray ate slowly, the way he eats now, like he has to think about each bite. He kept his socks on under the table.

After dinner Ray went to the recliner. He was asleep in 11 minutes.

Becca and I sat at the table with a second cup of coffee and she pulled something out of her purse.

It was a small white bottle with orange writing on the side.

She set it on the table between us.

She said, "Mom, I want to talk to you about something. I don't usually do this. I see a lot of stuff at work and I am not the kind of person who pushes things on people. But I have been watching Dad for the last 6 months and I need you to listen to me."

I listened.

She told me that one of the patients she'd cared for in the spring, an older man named Mr. Whitfield from Bartlesville, had Type 2 diabetes and bad neuropathy. He came in for unrelated reasons. But she'd noticed that his feet were not the feet of a diabetic with 14 years of neuropathy. They were warm. He had feeling in them. He told her his daughter had put him on amla 2 years ago, that he took it every morning with his blood pressure medicine, and that his neurologist had been baffled by how stable he'd been for so long.

Becca had never heard of it.

She looked it up that night at the nurses' station.

She read for 3 hours.

What she found, and what she explained to me at my kitchen table while Ray snored softly in the next room, is this.

Your nerves, especially the long nerves that run down to your feet and your hands, are some of the most energy-hungry cells in your entire body. They need a tremendous amount of cellular energy to maintain themselves. They need energy to keep their protective coating intact. They need energy to send signals back and forth. They need energy to repair the small damage they take every day.

That energy comes from your mitochondria. The little engines inside every cell.

In a diabetic body, what happens over years is that the high blood sugar creates oxidative stress, and that oxidative stress wears down the mitochondria. And once the mitochondria can't keep up, the nerves don't have the energy they need to maintain themselves.

That's when the protective coating starts to thin. That's when the signals start to go wrong. That's when the burning starts at 2 AM. That's when you can't feel your slippers.

The gabapentin and the Lyrica, Becca said, work on the signal. They quiet the noise the broken nerve is making.

They do nothing about why the nerve is broken.

The nerve is broken because the engines inside it ran out of fuel.

She told me about amla. She told me it's a fruit that grows in India. She told me it has been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years. She told me what got her attention was that it does two things at once. It helps activate something called AMPK, which is one of the main pathways your body uses to support mitochondrial function. So it can help the engines start running better. And at the same time it has one of the highest antioxidant profiles ever measured in a food, which matters because oxidative stress is what wore the engines down in the first place.

So you're putting fuel back in. And you're stopping the damage that was draining the tank.

Becca said, "Mom. I'm not telling you it's a miracle. I'm not telling you Dad's neuropathy is going to go away. I am telling you that for the first time since I have been watching him decline, I have read something that addresses what's actually happening inside him instead of just covering it up. And after Mr. Whitfield, I had to try it."

She slid the bottle across the table to me.

She said, "It's Alevia. It's the brand he was on. I bought one for him and one for you. I want you to try it together."

I sat there with the bottle in my hand and I thought about the slippers.

For 3 years we had been managing it. We had not been fixing anything. We had been quieting noise.

Nobody had ever once mentioned the engines.

I want you to understand something.

I am not a woman who buys things off the internet. I am not a woman who falls for fads. I have been married to an HVAC technician for 42 years and I have learned how to be skeptical about claims and salesmen and people who tell you they have the answer.

But my daughter is a hospice nurse.

And she had sat at my kitchen table and explained to me, in plain English, why the thing my husband was being treated for was not what was actually broken.

I started Ray on it the next Monday.

I didn't tell him what it was at first. I just put two capsules next to his metformin on the kitchen counter and I said, "Becca brought these. They're supposed to be good for circulation. Try them with me."

He looked at me over his reading glasses.

He said, "Sue. I love you. But I'm not taking another pill."

I said, "It's not a pill. It's a berry. Becca said try it. Please try it."

He said, "If I do it for a month and nothing changes, I'm stopping."

I said, "Fine."

He took it that morning.

Now I want to tell you what happened over the next 90 days, because this is the part I want to be careful about.

The first 2 weeks, nothing.

I was watching him like a hawk. I would ask him every night, can you feel the floor? Can you feel your socks? And he'd shake his head no and shrug and go back to the TV.

I almost gave up.

In week 3, he told me something at breakfast. He said, "I slept in the bed last night."

I'd been so out of it I hadn't even noticed. He hadn't slept in the bed in 4 months. He'd been in the recliner every night.

I said, "How was it?"

He said, "Feet didn't burn till 4."

That used to be 2.

In week 4, something happened that I will remember for the rest of my life.

I was washing dishes at the sink. Ray walked into the kitchen behind me. I heard him stop. I heard him say, "Huh."

I turned around.

He was standing on the tile floor.

In his slippers.

He looked at me. He looked down at his feet. He looked at me again.

He said, "Sue. I can feel them."

I want you to know that I cried at the sink with a soapy plate in my hand. I cried so hard I had to sit down on the kitchen floor.

He came over and sat down next to me. On the tile. In his slippers. And he held my hand for I don't know how long.

By week 6, the burning was down to once or twice a week instead of every night. He was sleeping in the bed. He was walking out to the back porch in the morning with the paper. He fed the birds.

By week 8 he went to Lowe's on a Saturday.

He came home with a piece of pine and a story about a guy he ran into who used to work at the same HVAC company he worked at in the late 80s.

By week 11 he was downstairs in the workshop building a birdhouse.

He told me last weekend he wants to make Eli a toy box for his 7th birthday next spring.

He said, "I want him to have something I made."

I am writing this from the kitchen table. Ray is downstairs. I can hear the sander.

He is still on his metformin. He is still on his gabapentin, but at a lower dose, which the doctor agreed to last month after his last appointment because his nerve function tests had improved.

Improved.

That word. After 3 years.

His neurologist actually asked him what changed. Ray told him. He said the doctor wrote it down on the back of a prescription pad.

I don't know what that doctor did with the note. But I know he wrote it down.

I am not going to sit here and tell you that my husband's diabetic neuropathy is cured. The doctor was very clear with us that we are still managing a condition. He is still a diabetic. He still has to test his finger at 6:40 AM. He still has to be careful.

But the engines are running.

He feels his slippers.

He sleeps in the bed.

He builds things again.

And I have my husband back.

If you are reading this and you are watching somebody you love retreat from their own life one piece at a time, if you are watching a husband or a father or yourself stop doing the things that made you who you are, if the doctor has told you that this is just how it is now and we just manage it, I want you to know there's another way to think about it.

The engines can be supported.

Alevia Amla is what Ray takes every morning. 2 capsules with his coffee. There are 30 servings in a bottle. It's shipped from the USA and made in the USA from amla that's sourced from where it grows.

They offer a 90-day money-back guarantee. You can use the whole bottle. You can use 3 bottles. You send them back and they refund you. No phone calls. No arguments.

Try it for 90 days. The same 90 days Ray tried it for.

Worst case, you send it back and you get your money. Best case, your husband walks out to the back porch in his slippers and feeds the birds.

P.S. I want to tell you something about Becca. She's been a hospice nurse for 11 years. She sees a lot of people at the end of things. She told me one time that the saddest thing she sees is not the dying itself. She said the saddest thing is the family that sits at the bedside and tells her how the patient was 5 years ago, how he used to fish, how she used to garden, how he used to dance, how she used to laugh, and Becca thinks, "Why did you wait? Why did you watch them disappear for 5 years before you got worried?" She told me that's why she gave me that bottle. She said she didn't want to be sitting at our kitchen table 5 years from now hearing me tell some other nurse about how Dad used to build things. She said she wanted to give us a chance to not be that story.

P.P.S. The 90-day guarantee is real. I asked. I called Alevia and asked them to spell it out for me. They said even if the bottle is empty, mail it back, full refund, no questions. That is not how any of Ray's prescriptions work. The Lyrica that made his ankles swell up like grapefruits and put 16 pounds on him did not come with a money-back guarantee. The gabapentin that left a running truck in the Walmart parking lot did not come with one. Nothing in our medicine cabinet does. The pharmacy industry does not refund you when their product makes you worse. Alevia does. That tells you something about who's confident in what they're selling.

P.P.P.S. Alevia is a small company. They run out. I've had to wait once already for a reorder. I now keep two bottles in the cabinet because I am not going back to October. I am not going back to dusty slippers. I am not going back to my husband retreating from his own life one piece at a time. If you have been watching somebody you love fade for too long, please don't wait another month. Please don't wait for the next thing to go. The slippers were Ray's first thing. The porch was second. By the time it was the workshop, I was losing him. Don't wait for the workshop.

P.P.P.P.S. Becca came down last weekend for dinner. Ray was downstairs sanding. She and I sat at the kitchen table the way we did in October. She said, "Mom. Dad's back." I said, "I know." She said, "Did you ever think this would happen?" I said, "No. I really didn't." She squeezed my hand and she said, "Mr. Whitfield's daughter told me when I asked her about the amla, she said, 'I just wanted to give Dad a chance.' That's what you did, Mom. You gave him a chance." That's all I'm asking you to do. Give the person you love a chance.

body_full:
If your knees pop and crackle like firecrackers, your hips ache so bad you can barely get out of bed, and they keep telling you it's "just arthritis"... 
I'm about to tell you exactly what they're hiding from you and why they'll NEVER tell you the truth.

And by the end of this, you're gonna be pissed.

Because there are three things happening right now:

1. Your joints are screaming at you that something's wrong
2. The medical system is gaslighting you into thinking it's normal aging
3. There's a billion-dollar industry that profits every single day you stay in pain

So let me tell you what happened with my sister, because her story is gonna open your eyes to how fucked up this really is.

For YEARS—and I mean like four straight years—my sister was dealing with this shit.

Her knees? 
She couldn't kneel down to play with her grandkids. 
Couldn't even think about gardening anymore—something she'd done her whole life. 
She's 58 years old, always been active, did yoga three times a week — and suddenly she's moving like someone twice her age.

By morning, her joints were so stiff she'd have to roll out of bed sideways and hold onto furniture just to make it to the bathroom. 
The first 30 minutes of every day felt like her body was made of concrete.

She stopped going to yoga. 
Stopped meeting her friends for walks. 
Started making excuses to avoid anything where people might notice she was struggling.

And the pain?

That deep, gnawing ache that never went away. 
She'd take Advil, Aleve, whatever—just to take the edge off. 
But it always came back. 
Every single day. 
Sometimes worse than the day before.

So obviously, she goes to doctors, right?

Multiple doctors. 
Her GP. 
An orthopedic specialist. 
We're talking thousands of dollars in appointments, X-rays, MRIs... the whole nine yards.

And you know what every single one of them told her?

"Your X-rays look normal for your age."

"It's just wear and tear."

"You need to lose some weight."

"Try physical therapy."

"Here's a prescription for anti-inflammatories."

ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES. 
This woman's joints are deteriorating and they're telling her to take stronger Advil.

But here's where it gets worse—and this is the part that made me start digging into what the fuck is actually going on.

They put her on prescription NSAIDs. 
Stronger stuff than you get over the counter.

You know what happened?

Her stomach started hurting. 
She got acid reflux. 
Started feeling nauseous after meals.

And her joints? 
Still aching.

The pills masked the pain for a few hours — but the underlying problem kept getting worse.

So at this point, I'm fucking furious.

Because I'm watching my sister—who's doing everything the doctors tell her, spending all this money, taking their prescriptions—get WORSE. 
Not better. 
Worse.

And that's when I started asking questions that nobody wants you to ask:

Why are doctors so quick to prescribe things that mask pain but never fix the root cause?

Why did the anti-inflammatories help temporarily but never actually stop the progression?

And why the fuck does nobody ever talk about what's ACTUALLY causing the cartilage in her joints to break down?

So I went down a rabbit hole. 
And I mean a DEEP rabbit hole.

I started researching why someone would have joints this painful when their X-rays looked "normal" — and every mainstream medical site was giving me the same bullshit answers. 

"It's arthritis. Lose weight. Take anti-inflammatories. Eventually you'll need surgery."

But then I found this research from doctors who actually study ROOT CAUSES instead of just symptoms.

And they were talking about something I had barely ever heard mentioned at any doctor's appointment.

Cellular energy depletion.

Now pause for a second.

You know what's insane?

Doctors will talk about inflammation. 
They'll talk about cartilage wearing down. 
They'll talk about bone-on-bone arthritis.

But nobody—and I mean NOBODY—ever talks about WHY your cartilage can't repair itself anymore.

And that's not an accident.

Because once you understand what happens to your cells after 40, you realize why anti-inflammatories don't fix anything long-term.

Here's what's actually happening in your joints:

Your cartilage—the cushioning between your bones—is made primarily of collagen. 
Strong, flexible protein fibers that act like shock absorbers.

When you're young, your body produces new collagen constantly. 
Repairs damage. 
Keeps everything cushioned and smooth.

But after 40? 
That production starts to crash.

Not because you're "getting old and that's just what happens."

But because your cells literally run out of the energy they need to make new collagen.

This energy is created by a molecule called NAD. 
It stands for nicotinamide adenine nucleotide.

Think of NAD like the battery pack that powers your cellular repair system.

When you're young, your cells are fully charged. 
They have the energy to produce collagen, repair damage, keep your joints healthy.

But by age 50? 
Your NAD levels drop by nearly 50%.

By 60? 
Even lower.

And here's the key thing most doctors will never tell you:

Without NAD, your cells can't produce collagen. 
Period.

It doesn't matter if you take collagen supplements. 
It doesn't matter if you eat protein. 
It doesn't matter if you do physical therapy.

If your cells don't have the energy to USE that collagen to repair your cartilage?

It's like having construction materials but no workers to build anything.

So here's what's happening in your joints right now:

One - Your body isn't producing enough new collagen to replace what's breaking down

Two - Even if you supplement with collagen, your cells don't have the NAD energy to use it for repairs

This creates a vicious cycle:

Your cartilage breaks down a little bit every day.

Your body can't repair it because your cells are running on empty.

The cartilage gets thinner and thinner.

Bones start rubbing closer together.

Inflammation kicks in as your body tries to protect the damaged area.

More breakdown. 
Less repair. 
More pain.

And all the while, doctors are just throwing anti-inflammatories at you—treating the symptom (inflammation) while completely ignoring the cause (cellular energy depletion).

Now you might be thinking: "Okay, so what about those joint supplements? Glucosamine? Chondroitin? Collagen peptides?"

Great question.

Those supplements give your body the raw materials—the building blocks.

But here's the problem:

They don't give your cells the ENERGY to use them.

It's like delivering lumber to a construction site with no electricity to run the power tools.

The materials are there. 
But nothing gets built.

That's why so many people try glucosamine or collagen and say "I didn't notice any difference."

It's not that the supplements are bad.

It's that they're only solving HALF the problem.

So when I learned all of this, I started looking for NAD supplements.

Because if NAD is the cellular energy that powers collagen production and joint repair, then THAT'S what my sister needed.

Not more anti-inflammatories.

Not more collagen peptides that her cells couldn't even use.

She needed to recharge her cellular batteries so her body could actually repair itself.

And here's where it gets interesting:

NAD research isn't new. 
Scientists have known about it for decades.

There are hundreds of studies showing that NAD levels decline with age and that restoring them can improve cellular function across the board—including in joint tissues.

Some researchers literally call NAD "the fountain of youth molecule."

But you'll never hear a mainstream doctor mention it.

Why?

Because there's no pharmaceutical drug version they can patent and sell for $500 a month.

NAD precursors—the supplements that boost NAD levels—are natural compounds. 
They can't be patented.

There's no money in telling you to fix your cellular energy.

There IS money in keeping you on anti-inflammatories, pain pills, and eventually joint replacement surgery.

See how that works?

So I finally convince my sister to try NAD supplementation.

And for the first time in four years, something actually made sense to her.

But here's the problem we ran into...

There are a million NAD supplements out there. 
Different forms. 
Different doses. 
Different quality levels.

Some use NAD precursors that barely get absorbed.

Some use doses so low they're basically useless.

Some are made by companies with zero third-party testing—you have no idea if what's on the label is actually in the bottle.

And she was spending a fortune trying to figure out which one actually worked.

But you know what? 
She found one that did. 
And after about three weeks?

The morning stiffness started getting better.

After a month?

She could kneel down without that sharp pain shooting through her knees.

After two months?

She was back at yoga. 
Playing with her grandkids on the floor. 
Gardening again.

Her joints felt like they did ten years ago.

So now I'm thinking: Okay, this works. 
It's literally life-changing. 
But why is it so hard to find a quality NAD supplement that actually delivers results?

That's when I started researching supplement companies that specialize in NAD.

I needed to find one that:

Had clinical doses (not fairy dust amounts)
Was third-party tested for purity
Had actual science backing the formula
Wasn't charging an insane markup

And here's what I found:

They specialize in NAD+ supplements specifically. 
That's their focus.

They use Nicotinamide Riboside (NR)—which research shows is one of the most effective NAD precursors for actually raising cellular NAD levels.

They use clinical doses—the same amounts used in the studies showing joint health benefits.

They're third-party lab tested. 
No fillers. 
Made in the USA.

And they had actual doctors recommending them.

Over 150 doctors on Frontrow MD specifically recommend Vasozi NAD for patients dealing with joint issues and age-related cellular decline.

When my sister switched to Vasozi NAD, something clicked.
Because it wasn't just about reducing inflammation.
It was about giving her cells the energy they needed to actually REPAIR her joints.

Within the first week, she noticed her mental fog lifting—NAD powers brain cells too.
Within two weeks, the deep ache in her knees started fading.
By three months?
Her body had time to produce new collagen. 
Her body's natural repair systems started working again. 

She got her life back.

This is what they don't want you to know about.

Because the second you restore your cellular energy and your joints start repairing themselves?

You don't need their anti-inflammatories anymore.
You don't need their pain pills.
You might not even need that $40,000 knee replacement they've been pushing.

Your body starts doing what it used to do when you were younger.

Now here's the thing I need you to understand:

If you've been dealing with chronic joint pain—knees, hips, shoulders, whatever—and nothing has worked long-term?

It's not because you're "just getting old."
It's not because you need to lose weight.
It's not because you're "doing too much."

It's because your cells don't have the energy to repair your joints. 
And nobody is addressing it.

They're treating the inflammation—the symptom.

Go get it.

hook_first_line: Migraines have NOTHING to do with stress, dehydration, or just "bad headaches." Let me explain.
body_full:
Migraines have NOTHING to do with stress, dehydration, or just "bad headaches." Let me explain.
I have been a Neurologist for over 15 years, and I suffer from migraines myself. Let me tell you about my patient Rachel.
She's 47, mother of two, and for the past four years every single day has started the exact same way.
She opens her eyes, and before she even sits up, she checks. Is it there? The pressure behind her right eye. The tightness wrapping around her temple. The dull, heavy throb at the base of her skull.
It's always there.
Some mornings it's a 5 and she can push through. Most mornings it's a 7 or 8 and she's already calculating which parts of her day she'll have to cancel.
Her kids have stopped asking if Mom is coming to their events. Her husband stopped asking how she feels. She stopped telling the truth years ago anyway. "I'm fine."
After four years of this exact cycle, she'd tried everything...
First, she lived on Excedrin and Advil. Popping them 4 to 5 times a week. They'd take the edge off for a few hours, but the migraines kept coming back harder. Nobody told her that using painkillers more than three days a week can actually cause MORE migraines. It has a name: Medication Overuse Headache. The pills she thought were saving her were trapping her in a cycle.
Next, her doctor put her on Topamax for prevention. It made her forget words mid-sentence. Her coworkers thought something was seriously wrong with her. She couldn't think straight, couldn't focus, couldn't function. And she still had the migraines.
Then Propranolol. Then Amitriptyline. Then Triptans that worked for a while and then stopped. Then Botox: 31 injection sites across her forehead, temples, and neck every twelve weeks. Five rounds. Nothing changed.
So she finally came to see me.
I spend my days treating migraine cases that most doctors never get clear answers for. Chronic migraine, migraine with aura, vestibular migraine, hemiplegic migraine, I've seen it all.
When I examined Rachel and reviewed her history, I could tell right away what was happening.
And this is the part almost no one explains to patients...
Her trigeminal nerve was chronically sensitized. Firing pain signals before the headache ever started.
I explained to her that a migraine doesn't begin with pain. Pain is the last stage. The migraine actually starts 20 to 40 minutes earlier, when the trigeminal nerve, the largest nerve in your head, running from the base of your skull through your temples and behind your eyes, becomes activated and starts sending cascading pain signals through your entire head.
By the time you feel the throbbing, that nerve has been firing for almost an hour.
And that's the reason nothing she'd tried had worked.
Because you can't fix a nerve problem with pills that take 30 to 45 minutes to reach your bloodstream.
By the time the Excedrin dissolves, gets absorbed through your stomach lining, enters your bloodstream, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and reaches the pain receptors... the migraine is fully established. You're an hour behind.
And you can't fix a nerve that fires at the surface of your skin with medications that work systemically through your blood. The delivery method is wrong. You're sending relief to the wrong place, arriving at the wrong time.
The problem was that Rachel needed to calm that nerve at the source. Directly. Immediately. The moment it starts firing, not 45 minutes later.
I could see the frustration on her face. She'd spent thousands of dollars and four years of her life. She asked me if there was anything that actually worked for this.
And that's when I told her about something I'd been developing.
See, I'd been seeing the same pattern over and over again in my practice. Patients with chronic migraines who weren't getting relief from traditional methods. Smart, desperate women who'd tried everything. And I kept coming back to the same observation:
Every treatment was trying to stop a migraine that was already fully activated. Nobody was addressing the nerve at the moment it starts firing.

All five working together, applied directly to where the trigeminal nerve lives, at the moment the migraine begins. Not 45 minutes later through your bloodstream. Seconds later, at the source.

First time, she felt the familiar pressure starting behind her right eye on a Tuesday afternoon. Instead of reaching for the Excedrin, she rolled Florus across her temples and behind her ears. The cooling hit within seconds. The pressure didn't escalate. It peaked at a 3 and faded by dinner.
She sat there waiting for it to come back. It didn't.

Over the past few years, over 7,405 migraine sufferers have tried it. Women and men who had the exact pattern Rachel had. Years of failed treatments. Dozens of medications. Doctors who said "we've tried everything."

hook_first_line: Alcohol is the most effective ADHD medication nobody prescribes.
body_full:
Alcohol is the most effective ADHD medication nobody prescribes.

That is the problem.

Because for an ADHD brain, alcohol works frighteningly well at first. It slows the racing thoughts. Softens the overwhelm. Lowers inhibition. Forces a dopamine release. Pulls the nervous system into a gear it has not been in all day.

For one hour, the brain finally feels quiet.

That relief is staggering when you have spent your whole life mentally overstimulated.

Which is exactly why the habit becomes the problem.

My name is Dr. Alan Mercer. I am writing this on a Sunday afternoon for one reason.

My younger brother Daniel died at 33 from complications of chronic alcoholism.

He had ADHD his entire life. Nobody ever diagnosed it. Nobody ever connected it to the drinking. Not his pediatrician. Not his college doctor. Not the three different specialists my parents took him to in his twenties.

I am a doctor. I missed it too. For 25 years.

I closed my family medicine practice three years ago and opened the Dopamine Restoration Clinic because of what I am about to tell you. It is what I now tell every adult who sits across from me suspecting they are drinking, or scrolling, or snacking, or smoking, more than they should be, and quietly hating themselves for it.

You are not weak.

You are not "an addict."

You are running a brain that has spent decades trying to medicate a chemical deficit nobody ever named for you. And alcohol happens to be the cheapest, most socially accepted version of that medicine on the planet.

Daniel was the smart one in our family.

The one teachers wrote home about. The one who could read 400 pages in two days and remember every character a year later.

He had his first beer at 16 the night of the spring play. He was throwing up backstage from anxiety. A senior handed him a flask. He drank it. He walked on stage. He said his lines.

That night he told me something I did not understand for 25 years.

"Alan. The volume just... went down. For the first time in my life it was quiet in my head for an hour."

By 19 he was the guy at every party who could drink anyone in the room under the table and walk out without slurring. The family legend. "Daniel doesn't get hungover."

By 24 he had built a construction company. Six employees. Never missed a Monday. Kept a fifth of vodka in his truck console.

By 28 my mother walked in on him at his birthday and noticed his hand was shaking before he picked up the glass.

He had been called "high functioning" his entire adult life.

He had been quietly drinking, for 17 years, to feel like the rest of us already felt sober.

At his service my father turned to me at the church door after the last person had left, and said something I have never been able to put down.

"For 28 years we told ourselves he just liked to drink, Alan. We were wrong the whole time."

Here is what almost nobody in mainstream psychiatry will tell you out loud.

Your brain runs on a chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is your inner volume knob.

It is what lets you sit through a meeting without your foot bouncing. What lets you watch a slow movie without checking your phone. What quiets the voice telling you that you are behind, you are failing, you are not as smart as everyone in the room thinks you are.

In an ADHD brain, that chemical runs 30 to 40 percent below baseline. Sparser receptors. And the small amount that does get released gets broken down too quickly by an enzyme before the brain can actually use it.

An ADHD brain lives every day in a state of chronic dopamine starvation. With the volume turned up on every sensory input the rest of the world manages to ignore.

Now think about what alcohol does the first time it crosses into the brain.

It forces a fast dopamine release. Quiets the nervous system. Silences the imposter voice. Pulls the brake on the inner monologue that has been running since 6am.

For a neurotypical person, two drinks feels like a buzz.

For an ADHD brain, two drinks feels like arriving.

Like finally becoming the version of yourself you have always suspected was in there somewhere.

That is not escape. That is regulation.

The problem is that alcohol does not heal the ADHD brain. It borrows the calm from tomorrow.

The next morning brings lower dopamine. More anxiety. Brain fog. Emotional volatility. Worse sleep. Stronger cravings by 4pm.

So the same exhausted brain reaches for the same medicine again the next evening.

That is the loop millions of high-functioning ADHD adults live inside, sometimes for decades, while quietly blaming themselves for lacking discipline.

I genuinely believe most of these people are not addicted to alcohol.

They are addicted to finally feeling normal for an hour.

That is the version of this that does not show up in the AA literature, and does not get diagnosed in a 12 minute appointment, and does not get fixed by another round of willpower.

It is the version that killed my brother. And it is the version that walks into my clinic almost every week now.

Three years ago, after Daniel, I started chasing the chemistry side of this seriously.

I had been a family doctor for 12 years and I knew none of it.

I ended up in a basement lab in Boulder, Colorado, across from a 71-year-old PhD neurochemist who had been studying dopamine for four decades. Two of her papers had never been cited in any psychiatric textbook I had ever opened.

When I told her about Daniel, she listened until I was finished. Then she said something I have been repeating to patients ever since.

"Your brother did not have an alcohol problem. He had a dopamine problem he learned to manage with the cheapest sedative the world makes legal."

She told me there are four things that determine whether an ADHD brain reaches for the bottle at 5pm or just... does not.

The first is the actual raw material the brain uses to manufacture dopamine in the first place. An amino acid called L-Tyrosine. Almost no adult eats enough of it in any usable form from food alone. Without it, the rest is moot.

The second is the cofactor the brain needs to actually convert that raw material into dopamine. The active form of B6. The body either has it or it does not.

The third is the enzyme that breaks dopamine down too quickly inside an ADHD brain. The one that pulls the chemical away before the brain ever gets to feel it.

She told me there is exactly one botanical with serious human research behind gently slowing that enzyme down. Rhodiola Rosea. But only when it is standardized properly. The cheap drugstore extracts are almost decorative.

And the fourth is the overstimulation underneath all of it. The reason the music is too loud, the lights are too bright, the meeting room is unbearable.

Two things quiet that, gently, without sedation. L-Theanine. Magnesium. They turn the volume knob down without putting you to sleep.

There is also a slower piece, she said. Vitamin D3, acting like a neurosteroid in the brain. The thing that makes the improvements compound over months instead of plateauing at week six. Most people skip it because it is not flashy. It is the most important one for the long game.

I asked her if anyone had built this in one place.

She paused.

Then she told me her former graduate student had spent four years quietly getting it right with a small supplement company. Two capsules a day. Everything we had just talked about, in the exact forms and exact doses she had walked me through.

She wrote the name on the back of a notebook.

CTRL.

I went home that night and read everything I could find on it before I made any decision.

What I cared about was simple. It was natural. It was not a stimulant. It would not interact with the medications most of my patients are already on. And the formula was specifically designed around the brain's own dopamine pathway, instead of overriding it the way Adderall does.

That last part mattered to me more than anything else after watching Daniel. The whole problem with the prescription stimulant model is that it floods the system and the brain downregulates to protect itself. By year three the patient is on twice the dose with half the effect.

CTRL works the opposite way. It is designed to feed the system, not flood it. The raw materials. The cofactors. The two compounds that take the brain out of seeking mode without sedating it. And the long-term piece that lets the improvements compound instead of plateauing.

That is the whole formula. Nothing in it the brain becomes dependent on. Nothing in it the body has to come down from at the end of the day. Nothing in it that someone in early sobriety, or on antidepressants, or pregnant, or anything else, has to white-knuckle around.

It is designed to do one thing. Quietly rebuild what was always supposed to be there.

So I put myself on it for two months before I gave it to a single patient.

By day 9 I was sitting through a 90-minute charting session without reaching for my phone for the first time in 8 years.

By day 21 I had stopped pouring the second glass of wine after dinner.

Not because I willed myself to stop. The pull was just... not there.

It did not feel like I had taken something.

It felt like something had finally stopped being missing.

That was eleven months ago.

A 33-year-old patient from my clinic called me a few weeks after her first appointment with me. She had been sober for 23 days. Not white-knuckling. Just not reaching for it.

She cried for most of the phone call.

Then she said something that has stayed with me.

"I did not know being normal was supposed to feel this quiet."

That phone call is part of why I finally sat down to write this.

If you have ever quietly wondered why one drink turns into four without you really deciding...

If you have spent years blaming your "addictive personality" because nobody has handed you a better word...

If the calm you are chasing in a bottle is a calm you have never been able to find anywhere else...

The word is dopamine.

The chemistry is fixable.

And once you understand what the alcohol was actually doing for your brain, you can finally stop hating yourself for needing relief so badly.

You were not drinking because you were weak.

You were drinking because you were starving.

Chemistry, unlike character, can be repaired.

If something in this hit close, this is where I would start:

https://try-balanced.com/pages/ctrl-lp-all

— Dr. Alan Mercer, Dopamine Restoration Clinic

P.S. I am not affiliated with the company that makes CTRL. I do not get paid to mention it. I write things like this on Sunday afternoons because the patients I cannot fit into my schedule deserve the same answer the patients in my schedule get. Daniel deserved that answer 17 years ago. He never got it. This is the closest I can come to giving it to someone else now.

P.P.S. If you are reading this and you do not have ADHD but you recognize yourself in the pattern anyway... that is also worth paying attention to. A huge percentage of the adults I treat for this never had a formal diagnosis. They just spent their whole lives reaching for something to make the volume go down, and never had a name for why.

hook_first_line: If your knees pop and crackle like firecrackers, your hips ache so bad you can barely get out of bed, and they keep telling you it's "just arthritis"...
body_full:
If your knees pop and crackle like firecrackers, your hips ache so bad you can barely get out of bed, and they keep telling you it's "just arthritis"... 
I'm about to tell you exactly what they're hiding from you and why they'll NEVER tell you the truth.

And by the end of this, you're gonna be pissed.

Because there are three things happening right now:

1. Your joints are screaming at you that something's wrong
2. The medical system is gaslighting you into thinking it's normal aging
3. There's a billion-dollar industry that profits every single day you stay in pain

So let me tell you what happened with my sister, because her story is gonna open your eyes to how fucked up this really is.

For YEARS—and I mean like four straight years—my sister was dealing with this shit.

Her knees? 
She couldn't kneel down to play with her grandkids. 
Couldn't even think about gardening anymore—something she'd done her whole life. 
She's 58 years old, always been active, did yoga three times a week — and suddenly she's moving like someone twice her age.

By morning, her joints were so stiff she'd have to roll out of bed sideways and hold onto furniture just to make it to the bathroom. 
The first 30 minutes of every day felt like her body was made of concrete.

She stopped going to yoga. 
Stopped meeting her friends for walks. 
Started making excuses to avoid anything where people might notice she was struggling.

And the pain?

That deep, gnawing ache that never went away. 
She'd take Advil, Aleve, whatever—just to take the edge off. 
But it always came back. 
Every single day. 
Sometimes worse than the day before.

So obviously, she goes to doctors, right?

Multiple doctors. 
Her GP. 
An orthopedic specialist. 
We're talking thousands of dollars in appointments, X-rays, MRIs... the whole nine yards.

And you know what every single one of them told her?

"Your X-rays look normal for your age."

"It's just wear and tear."

"You need to lose some weight."

"Try physical therapy."

"Here's a prescription for anti-inflammatories."

ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES. 
This woman's joints are deteriorating and they're telling her to take stronger Advil.

But here's where it gets worse—and this is the part that made me start digging into what the fuck is actually going on.

They put her on prescription NSAIDs. 
Stronger stuff than you get over the counter.

You know what happened?

Her stomach started hurting. 
She got acid reflux. 
Started feeling nauseous after meals.

And her joints? 
Still aching.

The pills masked the pain for a few hours — but the underlying problem kept getting worse.

So at this point, I'm fucking furious.

Because I'm watching my sister—who's doing everything the doctors tell her, spending all this money, taking their prescriptions—get WORSE. 
Not better. 
Worse.

And that's when I started asking questions that nobody wants you to ask:

Why are doctors so quick to prescribe things that mask pain but never fix the root cause?

Why did the anti-inflammatories help temporarily but never actually stop the progression?

And why the fuck does nobody ever talk about what's ACTUALLY causing the cartilage in her joints to break down?

So I went down a rabbit hole. 
And I mean a DEEP rabbit hole.

I started researching why someone would have joints this painful when their X-rays looked "normal" — and every mainstream medical site was giving me the same bullshit answers. 

"It's arthritis. Lose weight. Take anti-inflammatories. Eventually you'll need surgery."

But then I found this research from doctors who actually study ROOT CAUSES instead of just symptoms.

And they were talking about something I had barely ever heard mentioned at any doctor's appointment.

Cellular energy depletion.

Now pause for a second.

You know what's insane?

Doctors will talk about inflammation. 
They'll talk about cartilage wearing down. 
They'll talk about bone-on-bone arthritis.

But nobody—and I mean NOBODY—ever talks about WHY your cartilage can't repair itself anymore.

And that's not an accident.

Because once you understand what happens to your cells after 40, you realize why anti-inflammatories don't fix anything long-term.

Here's what's actually happening in your joints:

Your cartilage—the cushioning between your bones—is made primarily of collagen. 
Strong, flexible protein fibers that act like shock absorbers.

When you're young, your body produces new collagen constantly. 
Repairs damage. 
Keeps everything cushioned and smooth.

But after 40? 
That production starts to crash.

Not because you're "getting old and that's just what happens."

But because your cells literally run out of the energy they need to make new collagen.

This energy is created by a molecule called NAD. 
It stands for nicotinamide adenine nucleotide.

Think of NAD like the battery pack that powers your cellular repair system.

When you're young, your cells are fully charged. 
They have the energy to produce collagen, repair damage, keep your joints healthy.

But by age 50? 
Your NAD levels drop by nearly 50%.

By 60? 
Even lower.

And here's the key thing most doctors will never tell you:

Without NAD, your cells can't produce collagen. 
Period.

It doesn't matter if you take collagen supplements. 
It doesn't matter if you eat protein. 
It doesn't matter if you do physical therapy.

If your cells don't have the energy to USE that collagen to repair your cartilage?

It's like having construction materials but no workers to build anything.

So here's what's happening in your joints right now:

One - Your body isn't producing enough new collagen to replace what's breaking down

Two - Even if you supplement with collagen, your cells don't have the NAD energy to use it for repairs

This creates a vicious cycle:

Your cartilage breaks down a little bit every day.

Your body can't repair it because your cells are running on empty.

The cartilage gets thinner and thinner.

Bones start rubbing closer together.

Inflammation kicks in as your body tries to protect the damaged area.

More breakdown. 
Less repair. 
More pain.

And all the while, doctors are just throwing anti-inflammatories at you—treating the symptom (inflammation) while completely ignoring the cause (cellular energy depletion).

Now you might be thinking: "Okay, so what about those joint supplements? Glucosamine? Chondroitin? Collagen peptides?"

Great question.

Those supplements give your body the raw materials—the building blocks.

But here's the problem:

They don't give your cells the ENERGY to use them.

It's like delivering lumber to a construction site with no electricity to run the power tools.

The materials are there. 
But nothing gets built.

That's why so many people try glucosamine or collagen and say "I didn't notice any difference."

It's not that the supplements are bad.

It's that they're only solving HALF the problem.

So when I learned all of this, I started looking for NAD supplements.

Because if NAD is the cellular energy that powers collagen production and joint repair, then THAT'S what my sister needed.

Not more anti-inflammatories.

Not more collagen peptides that her cells couldn't even use.

She needed to recharge her cellular batteries so her body could actually repair itself.

And here's where it gets interesting:

NAD research isn't new. 
Scientists have known about it for decades.

There are hundreds of studies showing that NAD levels decline with age and that restoring them can improve cellular function across the board—including in joint tissues.

Some researchers literally call NAD "the fountain of youth molecule."

But you'll never hear a mainstream doctor mention it.

Why?

Because there's no pharmaceutical drug version they can patent and sell for $500 a month.

NAD precursors—the supplements that boost NAD levels—are natural compounds. 
They can't be patented.

There's no money in telling you to fix your cellular energy.

There IS money in keeping you on anti-inflammatories, pain pills, and eventually joint replacement surgery.

So I finally convince my sister to try NAD supplementation.

But here's the problem we ran into...

There are a million NAD supplements out there.

Different quality levels.

Some use NAD precursors that barely get absorbed.

Some use doses so low they're basically useless.

Some are made by companies with zero third-party testing—you have no idea if what's on the label is actually in the bottle.

And she was spending a fortune trying to figure out which one actually worked.

But you know what? 
She found one that did. 
And after about three weeks?

After a month?

After two months?

She was back at yoga. 
Playing with her grandkids on the floor. 
Gardening again.

Her joints felt like they did ten years ago.

So now I'm thinking: Okay, this works. 
It's literally life-changing. 
But why is it so hard to find a quality NAD supplement that actually delivers results?

That's when I started researching supplement companies that specialize in NAD.

I needed to find one that:

Within the first week, she noticed her mental fog lifting—NAD powers brain cells too.

By three months?

This is what they don't want you to know about.

Because the second you restore your cellular energy and your joints start repairing themselves?

You don't need their anti-inflammatories anymore.

Now here's the thing I need you to understand:

hook_first_line: My manager took my keys off me in a meeting room because two people on my own team had put it in writing that they thought I was drinking at my desk. I have not had a drink in eleven years.
body_full:
My manager took my keys off me in a meeting room because two people on my own team had put it in writing that they thought I was drinking at my desk. I have not had a drink in eleven years.

He would not look at me. He looked at the table and said, "Denise will run you home. We will be in touch about a meeting."

I'm Karen, I'm 44, and I live in Nottingham. I run a customer service team of nine at a distribution place off the ring road, or I did, and I have been there fourteen years.

I am writing this for anyone who is being quietly written off at work, or at home, or by their own GP, while they know with everything they have that something is physically wrong with them. Please read all of it, because the answer was not anywhere near where any of us were looking, me included.

My dad drank. That is why I stopped at thirty three and never went back. Not one glass, not at Christmas, not at my own fortieth when everybody kept trying to put a prosecco in my hand. Ellie is thirteen and Sam is nine and neither of them has ever seen their mum with a drink.

So when Denise drove me home that afternoon and neither of us said a word for twenty minutes, I sat there with my lanyard in my lap and worked out how I was going to tell Mark that I had been sent home for being drunk.

The worst part is that I understood why they had written it.

It had been coming on for about eighteen months.

It started with the tiredness. Not tired the way a working mum is tired. Empty. I would sleep eight hours and wake up like somebody had unplugged me in the night. I would sit on the edge of the bed at half six with my hands on my knees, working out in my head whether I could physically stand up and get in the shower.

I stopped doing the tea on a Wednesday. Mark took it over and never made a thing of it, which somehow made it worse.

Then the bloating. Flat when I woke up. By four in the afternoon my waistband was cutting a line into me and I was sat at my desk with my jumper pulled down over the top button, undone underneath where nobody could see. I stopped tucking anything in. I bought two pairs of trousers a size up in March and by June they were tight by teatime as well.

Then the fog, and the fog is what finished me, because the fog happened in front of people.

I stood up in a Monday morning meeting, in the middle of a sentence about our delivery times, and lost the whole thread of it. Nine people looking at me. There was a graph on the screen behind me and I could not have told you what it was measuring. I said, "Sorry, give me a second." Then I stood there and said nothing for what felt like a minute.

I sent a client a price list with three of their prices wrong on it and did not spot it until they rang.

I called a lad on my team Chris for a fortnight. His name is Craig. I had known him six years and been to his wedding.

I walked into the filing cabinet by the printer twice in one week. Not a stumble, a proper walk into it, hip first, hard enough that I had a bruise the colour of a plum. My balance had gone strange and there was no way of saying that out loud to anybody without sounding like I had lost it.

And my words started slurring in the afternoons. That is the honest truth of it. Around half two, three o'clock, my mouth would get slow and heavy and I could hear myself doing it and could not stop it happening. A woman who is grey in the face, who walks into furniture, who slurs after lunch and keeps disappearing to the toilet. I know what that looks like. I have lived with what that looks like since I was a child.

The 3am waking started around the same time. Wide awake at three, every single night, heart going like I had run up the stairs. Then lying there in the dark listening to Mark breathing until the alarm went.

My hair was coming out in the shower. Handfuls of it, wound round my fingers, and I got into the habit of pushing it down into the plughole with my thumb so Mark would not see how much there was.

I lost about a stone without trying and I looked worse for it, not better. My face went hollow round the eyes. My mum said, "Are you actually eating, Karen," on the phone and I snapped at her and put the phone down, then sat in the car on the drive and cried for ten minutes before I went in.

I snapped at Ellie for leaving a glass on the stairs. Properly shouted, over a glass. She went up to her room and shut the door and I stood at the bottom of the stairs with my hand on the bannister and could not make myself go up and say sorry, because I knew I would do it again the next day.

And I went to the doctor. Over and over.

Visit one: "You run a team, you have got two kids, you are run down. Try getting to bed a bit earlier."

Visit two, different GP: "Your bloods are all normal. It is probably stress. Would you consider a low dose antidepressant, just to take the edge off?"

Visit three, after the slurring started, and I will remember this one until the day I die. He sat forward and said, very kindly, "Karen, how much do you drink in an average week? Be honest with me, it is confidential in here." I said none. He wrote something down. Then he asked me the same thing again in a different way, about weekends, about whether I ever had one at home on my own. I have never wanted to get out of a room so badly in my life.

Visit four, private GP because I was desperate, two hundred and eighty pounds: "Adrenal fatigue and the start of perimenopause. Take magnesium and see if you can reduce your workload."

Visit five, gastroenterologist, three hundred and forty pounds, twenty five minutes: "It is IBS. Cut the onions out and get more fibre in."

So I did the fibre. For six weeks I ate like a rabbit and the bloating got so bad I could not do a seatbelt up properly and had to hold it off my stomach with my hand all the way to work.

I have added it up since. Two hundred and eighty for the private GP. Three hundred and forty for the gastro. Sixty eight pounds on a food intolerance test off the internet that told me to stop eating eggs. Nine months of probiotics at forty seven pounds a month. Just short of fourteen hundred pounds to be told, in five different ways, that there was nothing wrong with me.

Then occupational health rang me at home and asked whether I felt "able to be around the team at the moment". That was the phrase. I said yes and my voice went and I had to pretend the dog had barked.

Here is the bit I have not said out loud to many people. My nan had early onset dementia and died in a home in Beeston at sixty one. I can remember her calling me by her sister's name. So while HR were deciding whether I turned up drunk to my own meetings, I was lying awake at three in the morning certain I was going the same way she went, twenty years earlier than she did.

One night I got up and sat at the kitchen table with a notepad and wrote things down while it was quiet. Where the boiler paperwork is. Which of Sam's teachers to ring about his reading, because she is the only one who knows the plan. My passwords, in the order you would need them. What Ellie is actually like when she says she is fine.

I put it in a folder in the drawer where the batteries are and I did not tell Mark, because saying it out loud would have made it a real thing that was happening. Then I stood on the landing outside Sam's room for a while and went back to bed.

That is where I was in June. Signed off sick, waiting on a meeting with HR, and quietly getting my affairs in order at forty four.

The person who got me out of it was Denise. The same Denise who drove me home. She was one of the two who had put it in writing.

She turned up at mine on a Thursday with a bag of shopping and said, "I have got something to tell you and you are going to hate me." She told me she wrote the statement. She also told me she had regretted it from the second she watched me trying to get my seatbelt on outside my own house.

Then she put her laptop on my kitchen table and did the one thing not one person with a certificate on their wall had done in eighteen months.

She did not search "why am I so tired". She made me list every single thing. The bloating, flat in the morning and swollen by teatime. The exhaustion that sleep did nothing for. The fog. The slurring in the afternoons. The 3am waking with my heart going. The hair in the plughole. The weight coming off. The snapping. And she searched all of it together, at once, instead of one bit at a time in a ten minute appointment.

What kept coming back was intestinal parasites.

I nearly closed the laptop on her hands. I said, "Denise, we live in Nottingham, I hoover every day, do not be ridiculous." She said, "Just read it."

So I read it, and it was my last eighteen months, paragraph by paragraph.

The World Health Organisation estimates around one in three adults in the developed world is carrying an intestinal parasite. It has nothing to do with being dirty. You get them from undercooked meat, from bagged salad that was not washed properly, from the dog, from public toilets, from swimming pools. We took the kids to the pool at Center Parcs twice that year.

They attach to the gut wall and they take the iron and the B12 before your body ever gets near absorbing it. That is why my bloods came back sitting just inside normal while I felt like I was dying. I was eating, but I was not the one being fed. That was the tiredness that eight hours of sleep never touched.

They release waste into the bloodstream and it reaches the brain. That is the fog. That is standing in front of nine people with a graph behind me that meant nothing. That is the slurring at three o'clock, and the filing cabinet, and my nan's illness sat on my chest every night at 3am for no reason at all.

They inflame the gut lining. That is the bloating that gets a label slapped on it and sent home. IBS. Try more fibre.

They are most active at night. That is why it was three o'clock every night, on the dot, with my heart going.

And then the bit that made me furious. They hide behind a biofilm, a slime shield over the gut wall, and standard stool tests miss up to ninety percent of them. Every test I had was never going to find it. Not one of them was ever going to see it. Fourteen hundred pounds, eighteen months, and a formal investigation at work over something the tests are not built to pick up.

I was not lazy. I was not depressed. I was not drinking at my desk. Something was living in me and taking everything I put in my mouth.

So I did what everybody does first. I drove into town to the health shop and bought oregano oil for twenty two pounds because it was the one on the shelf at eye level.

Two weeks. Nothing. Not a flicker of anything.

Then I actually read the label. Eighteen percent carvacrol. Carvacrol is the active bit, it is what ruptures them and dissolves the biofilm, and you need eighty percent minimum to get through that shield. Most of what sits on a shelf is between fifteen and fifty percent. Under eighty and you have bought yourself expensive olive oil while the parasites sit behind their slime perfectly safe.

Denise found the one with the numbers right. Herbies Oregano+.

Eighty percent carvacrol from wild Mediterranean oregano. Cold pressed black seed oil in the same softgel for the thymoquinone, which stops them reproducing and helps flush them out. Both used for thousands of years, neither of them new. Third party lab tested. Nitrogen sealed so it does not oxidise on the way to you. No fillers and no oily burps, which mattered to me because the cheap stuff had me tasting oregano at four in the afternoon.

Two softgels every morning. That is all it is.

Day one, two of them with my tea. Bit of gurgling and that was it.

Day two and three I was in the bathroom a lot, and I am going to be honest with you because nobody was honest with me: it was poop, bad bacteria, and worms. Literally everything. Nobody warns you about the first two days.

Day six I am not going to describe in an advert. I sat down on the bathroom floor in my dressing gown with the door shut and I sobbed. Not from disgust. From relief. Because there it was on the porcelain, undeniable, after eighteen months of being told my bloods were normal and being asked how much I drink at weekends.

Mark came up and I would not let him in. Then I did. He sat on the edge of the bath and looked and said, "So it was real." It was real.

After those two days, honestly, I felt amazing.

End of week one my stomach was not thick and bloated by the evening anymore. I put on the trousers I had given up on and they were still done up at ten o'clock at night. I sat on the sofa with my hand on my stomach like an idiot, checking.

Week two I slept from eleven until half six. A whole night, all the way through. I woke up and lay there trying to work out what was different, and then I cried again, which is apparently all I did that month.

Week three the fog went. That is the only way I can say it. I read a full page of a delivery report and understood it the first time through. I called Craig by his own name. I had not felt properly awake since my thirties.

Week four the energy came back and that was the best part of the lot. Not coffee energy. I felt light, happy, full of power. I took Sam to the field after school and ran about with him instead of sitting on the bench with my coat done up watching him from a distance.

My skin went clearer and less oily as well, which I never asked for and did not expect. Ellie noticed it before I did and asked what I was using.

The snapping stopped. That is the one that actually matters to me. I have not shouted about a glass on the stairs since.

My mum drove over on a Sunday in August and told me off for twenty minutes about the state of my freezer and the fact that I had let the front hedge get away from me. I stood in my kitchen being nagged about a hedge and I could have hugged her, because in April she had been sat in that same chair asking Mark, in front of me, whether I had seen anybody about my memory.

I went back to work six weeks after they took my keys off me. I did the Monday morning meeting standing up, no notes, straight through it, and I could see two of them glance at each other.

Denise caught me in the car park after and stood there with her keys in her hand and said, "I put that in writing about you. I am never going to forgive myself for it." I told her she is the only reason I know what it was, and I meant it, and I still do.

My manager never apologised. He said, "You are looking well, Karen," and moved straight on to the rota. I have decided I can live with that.

The only problem now is I have had to buy new clothes, because the ones I bought a size up are hanging off me. The old trousers went down to the charity shop on the parade last month.

And I only do it once or twice a year now. That is all you need. It is all natural, so you are not on something for the rest of your life. Now I understand why so many people order it again.

One more thing, because I think it matters.

It is not only for people who ended up where I was, with an HR meeting pending and a folder in the battery drawer. Most of the reviews are the everyday version of it. The bloating that no diet shifts. The tiredness that coffee does not touch. The fog. The stomach that goes hard and thick by the evening and then is flat again in the morning. People take it and within a few weeks the misery they had quietly got used to just starts lifting.

You do not have to be accused of something in a meeting room before it is worth looking.

Nobody is paying me to write this. I do not work for them and I get nothing if you buy it. I am a 44 year old mum of two from Nottingham who nearly lost a job she had done for fourteen years, and who spent months believing she was going the way her nan went.

Herbies Oregano+ is eighty percent carvacrol from wild Mediterranean oregano, cold pressed black seed oil for thymoquinone in the same softgel, nitrogen sealed, third party lab tested, no fillers, no oily burps. Two softgels every morning.

Do not make my mistake with the cheap stuff. Fifteen to fifty percent carvacrol cannot get through the biofilm, and you will decide none of this works when the truth is you were never on a strong enough dose to find out.

There is a 30 day money back guarantee, so if you feel no different you send it back and you have lost nothing. That is genuinely how I talked myself into ordering, because I had already handed fourteen hundred pounds to people with certificates on the wall.

They are a small company and they sell out regularly. I am sorry if it is gone by the time you click. If it is showing below, it is in stock right now.

Karen

P.S. The folder is still in the battery drawer. The passwords, the boiler paperwork, the note about Sam's reading. Mark says I should put it in the bin and I probably will. I am keeping it a bit longer, because every time I go in that drawer for a battery I remember that eighteen months of my life were taken off me by something two softgels a morning sorted out in six days, while five different professionals looked me in the face and told me I was fine.

hook_first_line: I used to leave the gym with a headache more often than not.
body_full:
I used to leave the gym with a headache more often than not.

Not from the workout. From the noise. Six different speakers, someone's music bleeding into someone else's, the clang of plates, a trainer yelling reps two machines over. By the time I got to my last set I wasn't even focused on the muscle anymore, I was just trying to get out of there.

I always thought that was normal. Just what a gym sounds like. You push through it or you don't go.

I didn't realize how much it was draining me until I started wearing Life+ during my sessions. Not blocking everything out, that's the part I didn't expect. I can still hear my trainer, still hear if someone calls my name. It just takes the edge off. The sharp stuff. The stuff that used to leave me foggy an hour later.

First time I wore them on a lat pulldown set I actually laughed a little. It was quiet enough that I could hear myself breathing, count my own reps in my head instead of losing count over the noise. Sounds small. Wasn't small. That was the first workout in months I left feeling clear instead of drained.

Then I started wearing them everywhere else too. On the balcony in Bali, actually, just existing, drinking coffee, listening to the birds without the sound of scooters and construction three streets over cutting through everything. On flights. In the car when I need ten minutes of my own head before a call.

It's this weird kind of quiet that isn't silence. You're still in the world, still hearing it, just not getting hit by it.

I didn't think I needed that. I thought I just had low tolerance for noise, or that I was tired, or whatever excuse I gave myself. Turns out I was just absorbing way more sound than my brain wanted to deal with, every single day, and never doing anything about it.

Life+ became the thing I reach for before I even think about it now. Gym bag, always in there. Bag for flights, always in there. It's small enough that I forget it's with me until I need it, and then I'm so glad it is.

If you leave loud places feeling more tired than you should, if your ears are working overtime and you've just never noticed, try wearing these for one gym session. One. See if you notice the difference I did.
headline: The gym got quiet, and my head finally caught up

hook_first_line: I used to leave the gym with a headache more often than not.
body_full:
I used to leave the gym with a headache more often than not.

Not from the workout. From the noise. Six different speakers, someone's music bleeding into someone else's, the clang of plates, a trainer yelling reps two machines over. By the time I got to my last set I wasn't even focused on the muscle anymore, I was just trying to get out of there.

I always thought that was normal. Just what a gym sounds like. You push through it or you don't go.

I didn't realize how much it was draining me until I started wearing Life+ during my sessions. Not blocking everything out, that's the part I didn't expect. I can still hear my trainer, still hear if someone calls my name. It just takes the edge off. The sharp stuff. The stuff that used to leave me foggy an hour later.

First time I wore them on a lat pulldown set I actually laughed a little. It was quiet enough that I could hear myself breathing, count my own reps in my head instead of losing count over the noise. Sounds small. Wasn't small. That was the first workout in months I left feeling clear instead of drained.

Then I started wearing them everywhere else too. On the balcony in Bali, actually, just existing, drinking coffee, listening to the birds without the sound of scooters and construction three streets over cutting through everything. On flights. In the car when I need ten minutes of my own head before a call.

It's this weird kind of quiet that isn't silence. You're still in the world, still hearing it, just not getting hit by it.

I didn't think I needed that. I thought I just had low tolerance for noise, or that I was tired, or whatever excuse I gave myself. Turns out I was just absorbing way more sound than my brain wanted to deal with, every single day, and never doing anything about it.

Life+ became the thing I reach for before I even think about it now. Gym bag, always in there. Bag for flights, always in there. It's small enough that I forget it's with me until I need it, and then I'm so glad it is.

If you leave loud places feeling more tired than you should, if your ears are working overtime and you've just never noticed, try wearing these for one gym session. One. See if you notice the difference I did.
headline: The gym got quiet, and my head finally caught up
