body_full:
~Lily~
 
Okay, listen to me. I know I sound crazy, but I swear I’ve officially lost every ounce of self-control I ever had. Like completely, tragically, erotically gone.
 
If there’s a special kind of werewolf for girls who moan their best friend’s dad’s name while fingering themselves in hotel beds, then I’m already seated in the front row. VIP. Permanent reservation. No chance of redemption. I’m going straight there, soaked and smiling.
 
I don’t even care anymore. I’ve judged myself so many times I’ve run out of shame to spiral in. I already did the whole “Oh my goodness, I’m such a terrible person, I’m going to regret this forever,” thing—three times, actually.
Do you know when? Right after each overwhelming moment. Because yes, I’ve been lying here for over an hour now. Legs open. Tank top rolled up. My fingers are shiny.
 
My voice is wrecked. My thighs are sticky. I’m panting like an unclaimed Omega in heat, and all of it—all the moaning, the trembling, the insane whimpers that sound like I’m being exorcised—has been for one man.
 
Connor Blackwood.
 
Not just any man. My best friend’s father. Her Alpha dad. Her six-foot-something, silver-eyed, veiny-handed, gravel-voiced, emotionally unavailable, broad-shouldered, grumpy-as-heck- father figure whose scent alone makes my heart flutter.
 
The kind of man who makes my stomach flip and my cunt ache just by existing near me. He is dangerous in ways my body doesn’t want to survive.
 
He is temptation wrapped in muscle and dominance. And if I could choose anyone in the entire world to take my virginity, ruin my innocence, leave me utterly breathless the soul right out of my body with nothing but his knot and his hands on my hips—it would be him.
 
No protection. No mercy. Just full Alpha madness. I want to be split open. I want to be marked and filled and pinned and broken.
 
I want his voice in my ear saying “You’re mine now” while I scream into the pillow and beg him not to stop. I want to belong to someone so completely that I forget my own name and start worshipping his.
 
And yes, I am eighteen. I’ve said it once, but I’ll say it again because it matters. I am legal. I am grown. I keep repeating it like some unholy prayer because I still don’t feel grown when I’m soaked through my panties and thinking about the way his mouth looked around the edge of a beer bottle.
 
I don’t feel grown when I remember him getting out of the pool last summer, water dripping down his chest, dark hair slicked back, Alpha scent rolling off him so thick I almost passed out. 
I stood there frozen, legs tensed, face flushed, heart racing, and every cell in my body yearning to be seen.
And now here I am. Moments later. Still overwhelmed. Still aching with want. Still shaking. I feel like something wild has snapped inside me and now all that’s left is longing. I want him more than I’ve ever wanted anything, and the worst part is—I haven’t even gotten on the yacht yet.
Yes. That’s right. I am going on a luxury private cruise in less than twenty-four hours. A yacht. Eight passengers. Expensive food. Ridiculously rich people. And one dangerously excited little Omega—me— who is one strong presence away from losing all composure. 

 
And guess who invited me?
 
Bella. My best friend. The girl who has absolutely no idea that her sweet, smiley, innocent bestie has been soaking through her sheets for two years now imagining what it would feel like to choke on her daddy’s knot.
 
I know I should have said no. I should have been mature and responsible and respectful. I should have said I was busy this summer. I should have said my grandma died again. I should have said I have a yacht allergy.
 
But instead, I said yes. I said yes so fast I nearly screamed.Then I went home and packed every single daring little outfit I own. The red panties. The lace ones. The sheer ones. The crotchless ones I bought in secret even though I’ve never even kissed a guy before.
 
I packed them all for him.
 
Because I want him to see me. I want him to look at me and forget I was ever a little girl. I want his eyes to drop.
 
I want him to smell the shift in my scent. I want him to freeze. I want his composure to falter. I want his inner Alpha to growl and snap awake. I want him to lose control.
 
I stand in front of the mirror now, staring at myself as I close my eyes, I see it—the dock, the burning Spanish sun, the glint of the yacht, Bella squealing and running. And then I turn around.
 
And there he is.
 
Connor Blackwood.
 
Wearing white linen pants. A dark shirt half unbuttoned. Sunglasses pushed up in his hair. Arms crossed. That mouth in a straight, unreadable line. That scent. That power. That him. Maybe he’ll glance at me. Maybe he’ll say my name. Maybe he’ll say “Lily.”
 
And I’ll smile. I’ll act like I’m not soaking wet underneath this dress. Like I haven’t been dreaming about this moment with my fingers stuffed between my legs since I was sixteen.
 
~~~
 
I was still standing in front of the mirror like a psycho, one hand on my hip, the other flailing dramatically as I practiced how I’d bend over without making it look like I was seeking attention.
I kept shifting my stance, straightening my posture, tilting my head just right like, Oops, I dropped my drink—guess I’ll just bend down near you and pretend it’s not intentional. That kind of thing. My steps were light and bouncy. My outfit looked absolutely perfect. The fabric of my tank top caught the eye like it was asking to be noticed.

And listen, don’t you dare judge me. I know for a fact I’m not the only girl who’s ever done this. I know you’ve arched your back in front of your crush like you just happened to need a stretch. I know you’ve “accidentally” dropped something just to see if his eyes would follow.
 
So don’t even look at me sideways right now. I’m just being honest. I’m just brave enough to say out loud what your slick little cunt already knows — we’re all dirty when the right man walks in.
 
I was mid-squat, practicing how I’d moan a fake “oops” while pretending to pick up a lip gloss, when my phone buzzed on the bed.
 
Bella.
 
Oh. shoot.
 
I swiped to answer.
 
“Hello?” I tried to sound normal, but my voice came out breathy.
 
“Where the heck are you?” Bella shouted over the wind and the sound of water slapping the dock. I could hear seagulls, someone popping champagne, and a yacht horn blaring like it was laughing at me. “Lily, the captain’s literally about to untie the ropes! If you miss this cruise because you’re curling your lashes—”
 
“I’m on my way!” I spun in a panicked circle, like that would somehow teleport me closer. “I’m five minutes out. Like, literally.”
 
“That didn’t sound convincing.”
 
“Eight! Okay, maybe ten. But a really fast ten. Like a super excited ten.”
Bella groaned, but she was laughing. “You better move your cheeky little self. This is going to be the summer that changes everything. Spain. France. Italy. Greece. Do you know how many hot guys are already on this boat?”
 
I tried to laugh. It came out as a dying whimper. “Oh, I’m so ready.”
 
She giggled. “Good. Champagne’s already flowing, nobody brought rules, and my dad’s the only adult on board. But he’s so boring he doesn’t count. He’s probably already in a corner somewhere glaring at the ocean with a whiskey in one hand and a trauma in the other.”
 
My whole body went still.
 
Her dad.
 
Connor.
 
And then she said it.
 
“I think Rose put you in the suite next to his. So maybe try not to moan too loud when you’re playing with yourself, yeah?”
 
My stomach dropped. My legs buckled. My stomach tightened so hard I gasped. Her father’s room is next to mine?
 
I could actually die. Or combust. Or just melt into a puddle of slick and sinful thoughts and slide under his door like some heat-struck ghost begging to be touched.
 
“Lily?” Bella’s voice dragged me back. “You okay?”
 
“Y-yeah,” I said, breathless. “Just…processing.”
 
She cackled. “Don’t overthink it. Just get here. This yacht is ridiculous. It has levels. Like, actual upstairs-downstairs levels. King beds. Showers that could fit six people. Mood lighting. This whole thing feels like it was made for romance.”

I was already grabbing my bag, shoving my feet into sandals, yanking my damp panties back into place with trembling fingers. “I’m leaving right now.”
 
“Good,” she said. “Let’s make some sins we’ll never forget.”
 
She hung up.
 
And I just stood there, staring at myself in the mirror again, shaking from the inside out.. This was it. The beginning of everything. The summer that would destroy me in the best possible way.
 
Okay wait before I open this door, before I see him again, before I do the dumbest, filthiest thing I’ve ever done in my life—I need to say something.
 
To you.
 
Yeah, you. The one reading this with your thighs tight and your lip bitten so hard it’s basically bruised. Don’t even pretend you’re not already wet, because I know you are. You wouldn’t be here otherwise.
 
Welcome to my disaster.
 
No, scratch that.
 
Welcome to my chaotic, forbidden-feeling, heart-pounding descent into madness.
 
Because what’s coming? Is not cute. It’s not slow-burn. It’s not romance. It’s something you haven’t read before.
 
You better have your toy charged. The real one. The one that doesn’t stop until you’re crying and breathless. Because this story?
 
It’s not for the soft-hearted. It’s for the ones who love filth.
 
So be a good little troublemaker.
 
Flip the page.
 
And don’t say I didn’t warn you.
 
~Lily~

I’ve never sweat through a sundress before. Not like this. Not with the sun barely even up and my thighs already soaked from the way I’ve been rubbing them together in the back of this damn cab like some overheated, restless fool.

I’m trying so hard to look normal, to act like I’m just an innocent eighteen-year-old girl on a luxury yacht cruise with her best friend’s family, but every time I blink I see him.

I see the way he looked last summer, shirtless and wet, his muscles tight and flexing while he poured himself a drink by the pool like the world was his. I see the way his mouth curved when he said my name. 

I see the little silver ring on his pinky finger and the veins on his forearms and the deep, deep line between his brows that only comes out when he’s focused. 

And I don’t even know what he was focused on that day, but God, I pretended it was me. I walked around that whole villa in tiny shorts and no bra, pretending I didn’t feel his eyes burning into my back, and when I heard his bedroom door close late that night, I swear I touched myself so hard I saw stars.

And now? Now I’m back. I’m legal. I’m dripping through my lace panties. And I’m about to step out of this cab and face the man I’ve been obsessing over since before I even understood why my body reacted to his voice the way it does.

I lick my lips as the car rolls to a stop and my stomach does this wild, dangerous flip that makes my whole body buzz. 

This is it. This is the dock. This is the moment. The yacht is right there. Big and white and sparkling in the Spanish sun like it’s made of secrets, temptation, and scandal.

The crew is loading the last of the bags, the waves are lapping at the dock, and I can hear laughter and champagne corks popping somewhere on the upper deck, but none of that matters because as soon as the car door opens. 

I see him.

Connor.

Walking down the stairs of the yacht like a walking scandal in motion.
I don’t breathe. I don’t blink. I don’t move a muscle except for the way my knees nearly buckle at the sight of him. He’s not wearing a jacket.

His shirt is black and unbuttoned just enough to make me want to bite his chest, and it’s tucked into white linen pants that make his waist look lethal. 

His sleeves are rolled up to his elbows and his skin is tan and golden and glowing, and I swear if I die right now, I’ll die wet.

He doesn’t say anything at first. He just stops at the bottom of the steps and stares. Like he’s trying to figure out what the heck I’ve turned into since last summer. Like he knows I’m not a girl anymore. Like he can smell what’s happening between my thighs.

Because I’m pretty sure he can.

His eyes drag from my hair to my lips to the bare skin above my neckline, lingering on the gentle curve outlined by the thin straps of my white sundress. I didn’t wear extra layers. I didn’t want to. I wanted this. I wanted his eyes on me. And now that I have them, I swear my pulse is pounding so hard I might faint.

“Lily,” he says.

J
Just that. One word. My name. But the way he says it is low and slow, heavy with something he’s trying to hide, and it makes my entire spine freeze because oh my gosh, I am not okay. My stomach tightens. My throat goes dry.
My muscles tense so fast they hurt, and all I can think is that this man is standing six feet away from me and already my body wants to crawl into his hands.

“H-hi,” I whisper, trying to keep my voice from breaking, but it cracks anyway and I probably sound like a virgin in a porno. “Hi, Mr. Blackwood.”

His jaw tightens.

His eyes narrow just a little.

“Connor’s fine.”

And just like that, I know I’m not surviving this cruise.

Because that tone? That name? That casual drop of formality?

That’s an invitation. That’s him stepping over the line, even just an inch. That’s him saying I see you. That’s him saying you’re not a child anymore. That’s him giving me just enough to drown in.

“Connor,” I repeat, and the name tastes like sin on my tongue.

He stares a second longer, and for a split second, I see it — I feel it — the flash of heat in his eyes. The flare of Alpha tension in the air. The way his chest lifts just slightly like he had to breathe me in. I don’t even think he realizes he’s doing it. It’s instinct. Raw, primal instinct.

And my slick pulses between my legs like it knows what’s coming.

Then—of course—Bella bursts out of nowhere like a walking interruption, wrapped in pink sunglasses and excitement. She throws her arms around me before I can even process what just happened and starts squealing in my ear about champagne and rooms and how amazing the boys are upstairs.
“Oh my God, you made it!” she shouts, hugging me like she didn’t just interrupt a silent, full-body rush.  “I thought you were gonna miss it! The boat’s insane, Lily. You are not ready. Come on, come on, everyone’s waiting! Wait ‘til you see the rooms.”

She grabs my wrist and pulls me toward the ramp, still chattering about bikinis and drinks, and I have no choice but to follow her—legs like jelly, heart in my throat, my core buzzing and pounding at the fact that I just locked eyes with Connor Blackwood and survived.
Barely.
But I can feel him behind me.I can feel his eyes following me.
I can feel his control slipping — just a little.

And that’s all I need.

~~
Bella was talking so fast I can barely keep up. Something about drinks and the hot tub schedule and the couple who already hooked up in the downstairs cabin even though we literally just boarded. 

I nod. I smile. I say “Oh my God” and “That’s wild” and try to pretend like I’m not still clenching my thighs with every step because the back of my dress keeps brushing against me, and it’s making me imagine Connor standing just a little too close instead.

Then I see them.

The rest of the group.

Four of them are already gathered in the lounge chairs under the canopy — two guys, two girls, all tan and laughing and sipping cocktails like this is their fourth summer in Saint-Tropez. One guy has tattoos. One girl has gold hoops the size of my fists. Everyone looks older, cooler, more relaxed. And me?

I look like someone hiding an innocent secret, with a heartbeat so strong I might black out.

Bella points them out like she’s doing roll call. “Okay, that’s Tyler — he’s mine, don’t touch, I’ll murder you. That’s Chase and Courtney — they break up like three times a day, so just smile and nod. And that’s Daphne and Elia — they’re obnoxiously in love and you’ll probably want to push them overboard by Day Three.”

I wave. I smile. I nod. I say something polite. I don’t remember what.

Because my mouth opens and the next words that come out?

I want to kill myself the second I say them.

“Your dad looks really built.”

Oh my God.

Did I just say that?
I said that.
I actually said that.

Out loud.
To her.
To his daughter.
In public.
Surrounded by people.

I want to grab the words and stuff them back down my throat, but they’re already hanging there in the air, sticky and perverted and impossible to explain away. And Bella — bless her oblivious heart — just turns her head and raises one brow at me like she heard exactly what I said and she’s giving me a chance to walk it back before it gets weird.

I panic.

“I mean not, like, in a weird way,” I blurt, talking faster than my brain can process. “I’m just saying he looks like, you know, he takes care of himself. Like, fit. Like, for his age. Not that he’s old. I didn’t mean that. I just meant like, if he wasn’t your dad—and obviously he is—but if he wasn’t, people would definitely think he’s like, some hot ex-military guy who jogs shirtless through the woods or something. Not that I imagine him jogging. I mean, not often. Maybe once. Or twice.”

I want to drown myself in the sea. Right now. I’ll tie an anchor to my ankle. I’ll do it.

But Bella? Bella just laughs.

Like a full, honest laugh. She covers her mouth and everything.

“Oh my God, Lily,” she wheezes. “You’re such a weirdo.”

“I didn’t mean it like that,” I whisper, even though I 100% did and we both know it.

She waves it off. “It’s fine. Everyone says that. My friends used to call him ‘Alpha Daddy’ and I wanted to crawl into a hole and die.”

Alpha Daddy. He’s mine. 

My stomach tightens so hard I have to clench my jaw.

I laugh nervously, pushing my hair behind my ear and trying to pretend my face isn’t beet red. “Well… I mean… I get it. He definitely has that whole… power thing going on.”

She shrugs. “He works out every morning. Like obsessively. Gets up at 5 a.m., lifts weights, runs in the sand, fights imaginary people in the backyard like he’s training for war. He doesn’t even use headphones. Just… growls.”

Growls.

My brain explodes.

My entire body turns into one giant need.

My body throbs. My head tilts back. My eyes flutter so far I think I might faint from how intense it feels.
I keep making sounds. I can’t stop. I’m rocking into my palm like I’m possessed by feeling. My whole body is shaking, my chest is heaving, and I don’t even care if anyone hears me.
I want him to hear me. I want Connor to hear the way I say his name when I lose control. I want him to know how strongly I react just from thinking about him. I want him to know that he caused this.
My voice turns raw. My words break apart. It’s not even clear speech anymore.
“Ah—oh—yes—yes—”
I reach down and rub faster, tight, while my fingers move. I’m close.
“Please—”
I’m not even thinking anymore. I’m just asking.
And then it happens.
The release rips through me with so much force that I cry out. Actually cry out. Burying my face into the pillow and letting it out.
“Oh—yes—”

My legs snap shut around my hand as my body convulses. I cry into the pillow. My fingers curl. My cunt clenches so tight it aches. 

My toes point. My lips tremble. Slick floods my hand and I don’t stop. I keep rubbing. I keep moaning. I ride it out like my soul is on fire and only his name can put it out.

And then. 

Knock knock knock.

“Lily?”

My blood turns to ice.

I freeze. My body jerks like I’ve been electrocuted. My hand flies away from my body so fast I nearly slap myself.
My legs clamp shut. My breath gets stuck in my throat. My entire body is still trembling, still clenching, still damp and pulsing, but now I’m panicked. I’m wide-eyed. I’m caught completely off guard with my best friend standing on the other side of the door.
“Lily, are you in there?”
It’s Bella.
I stare at the ceiling like it might open up and swallow me. My body is still twitching. My skin is sensitive. I can smell myself in the air. The whole room smells like overwhelming emotion.
“Drinks are starting,” she says. “Rose said to tell everyone to come to the lounge.”
I slap my hand over my mouth, trying not to gasp.
I don’t move.
I don’t breathe.
I just sit there on the bed, shaking and overwhelmed, barely functional while the aftershock still echoes through my thighs and my best friend knocks on the door asking why I’m taking so long.
“Lily?”
Oh my God. Oh my God. Bella. That’s Bella. That’s her voice. Outside my door. My best friend. Standing there. Knocking. While I am literally lying here with my dress bunched at my waist, my clothes disheveled, and my fingers damp and shaking.
“Lily, are you in there?”
Yes. I’m in here. I’m in here mentally collapsing. I’m in here soaking the sheets with sweat and twitching from the aftereffects of the most intense release I’ve ever had in my life.
I’m in here gasping for breath with my legs still shaking and the word Daddy still wet on my lips like a thought I don’t know how to erase.
“Drinks are starting. Rose said to tell everyone to come to the lounge.”
Drinks. Right. Great. Yeah, let me just uncurl myself from this bed like a freshly wrecked mess and walk into a yacht full of people with the aftereffects of my breakdown clinging to my skin and Connor’s name still echoing in my skull like a memory I can’t shut up.
My whole body goes rigid. My face is on fire. I reach for the pillow and press it over my face like it might smother the humiliation surging through my bloodstream.
My center is still throbbing. My clothes are damp. There’s a wet patch on the sheets under me and my hand is shiny with moisture. 

I scramble up like a gremlin caught in the light. My dress is bunched up. My panties are twisted. My fingers are damp.  I wipe them frantically on the inside of my thigh, then gasp and regret it because my skin is too sensitive and I nearly moan again like an idiot.

“Yeah” I shout, voice way too loud and cracked. “I’m fine! I’m coming!”

No. Bad choice of words. Very bad.

“I mean, I’ll be there! I was just… changing!”

My voice breaks on the last syllable and I clap a hand over my mouth like that will somehow erase the fact that I probably sound like I just got railed by a ghost. My thighs are shaking. My hair is a mess. My whole body feels like I just got bred and left to soak.

I shove my panties back up, wince at how wet they are, then pull my dress down and try to straighten it even though it’s clinging to my skin like it’s aware of everything I just did.

I fan my face with both hands.

“Okay, okay,” I whisper to myself like a girl on the verge of an emotional breakdown. 
“You just lost control for a moment, Silly, and said his name loud enough for Poseidon to hear.
No big deal. Just walk out there. Smile. Pretend your body isn’t aching. Pretend your thighs aren’t still damp. Pretend you didn’t react so strongly you buried your face in the sheets like a flustered mess.”
I wipe the inside of my thighs with a towel. It’s warm. Moist. Smells like me now. I shudder. I’m never going to be the same again.
I take one last breath, glance at the wall that separates me from him, and whisper under my breath like a girl who has already accepted her fate.
“Let’s just hope I can walk straight.”
I pull the door open, and for one shining second, I think I’ve made it.
And then I slam face-first into something.
Hard.
I gasp. I stumble. My hand flies to the doorframe to steady myself. My chest brushes against cotton, and every cell in my body goes hot.
I look up.
And it’s him.
It’s Connor.
His hand is already on my arm to steady me, big and warm and rough, and my whole body reacts before I can stop it. My center tightens. My throat dries. My brain starts short-circuiting like someone poured water into my soul.
His eyes meet mine. I knew definitely I was done for.
Heck.
headline: Daddy Alpha, I’m In Heat | Dreame

hook_first_line: My nightly glass of wine was the one thing I refused to give up. Turns out I didn't have to give it up. I just had to replace what it was taking from me.
body_full:
My nightly glass of wine was the one thing I refused to give up. Turns out I didn't have to give it up. I just had to replace what it was taking from me.

Let me tell you how I figured this out because it changed everything.

For about four years I had this routine. Kids in bed by 8. Glass of red wine on the couch. Sometimes two if it was a hard day. Nothing crazy. I'm not a big drinker. I'm a mom with a full-time job and two kids under ten and the wine was my thing. My reward for surviving another day. The thing that finally made my shoulders drop.

And it worked. For about two hours. I'd feel relaxed. Warm. Calm. I'd go to bed feeling good. Fall asleep fast.

Then 3AM would hit.

Eyes open. Heart going. Brain already running through tomorrow. Did I sign the permission slip. Is there gas in the car. What am I making for dinner tomorrow. Did I respond to that email from my boss. Just noise. Stupid noise that my brain decided was an emergency at 3 in the morning.

I'd lie there for an hour sometimes two. Sometimes I'd fall back asleep around 4:30 and get maybe an hour before the alarm went off. Sometimes I didn't fall back asleep at all.

By morning I was wrecked. Puffy face. Dark circles. Short temper. I'd snap at my kids during breakfast and feel guilty about it the entire drive to work. I'd need two cups of coffee by 9AM just to feel like a person. By 3PM I was running on nothing.

And then by 8PM I'd pour the wine again because I was so fried from the day that I needed something to take the edge off. And the cycle would start over.

I thought this was just what life felt like at 43 with a demanding job and two young kids. I thought everyone felt like this. I thought the wine was helping me cope. I thought the 3AM wake-ups were stress. Or hormones. Or perimenopause. My doctor said it was probably all three. She said "Maybe cut back on the wine" but she didn't explain why. She just said it like a general suggestion. Like eat more vegetables.

So I ignored it. The wine wasn't the problem. The wine was the only good part of my day.

Here's what happened.

My sister-in-law is a nurse. She works in women's health. She was staying with us for Thanksgiving and we were sitting on the couch doing our wine thing and I said something about how I can't remember the last time I slept through the night. I said it casually. Like a fact about the weather. That's how normalized it had become.

She looked at me and said "How much wine do you drink?"

I said one or two glasses a night. Most nights.

She said "And when did the sleep problems start?"

I had to think about it. And I realized they started around the same time. About four years ago. When the wine became a nightly thing instead of a weekend thing.

She said "I'm not going to tell you to stop drinking. But I need to tell you what it's doing."

She explained it simply. She said every glass of wine is a diuretic. It makes your kidneys flush minerals. Magnesium is one of the first to go. And it's not just the flushing — alcohol also damages the lining of your gut so you absorb less magnesium from food the next day. So you're losing more and absorbing less. Every night.

She said magnesium is the mineral that tells your nervous system to stay calm. Without enough of it your body can't hold rest mode through the whole night. That's why the wine knocks you out at first — the alcohol is a sedative. But then at 3AM your nervous system snaps awake because it doesn't have the magnesium to keep the brakes on. And by that point the sedative effect has worn off so there's nothing keeping you down.

She said "The wine isn't helping you sleep. It's knocking you unconscious for four hours and then pulling the rug out."

That hit me hard. Because she was right. I was passing out, not sleeping. There's a difference and I'd been pretending there wasn't.

She said "You don't have to stop drinking. But you have to replace what it takes. Every night."

She gave me magnesium gummies. She said take two before bed. She said make sure it's a form your body can actually absorb because most of the cheap ones at the pharmacy go straight through you. Like swallowing a marble. Your body never opens it.

She'd brought a bottle with her because she takes them herself. She handed me two.

I took them that night. Had my wine. Took the gummies about 30 minutes before bed. Went to sleep.

I woke up at 6:10AM.

I just lay there staring at the ceiling because something felt off. Then I realized what it was. It was morning. Actual morning. I'd slept almost seven hours straight. On a Thursday. With a glass and a half of wine in me. That never happens.

Second night. Same thing. Wine. Gummies. Slept through.

By the fourth night something else happened. I woke up and my neck felt loose. I'd been waking up with stiff neck and sore jaw every morning for over a year. I thought it was my pillow. I'd bought three different pillows. Turns out it was never the pillow. I was clenching my jaw all night because my nervous system was locked in fight mode. The magnesium turned that off.

By the end of the first week I felt like a different person. And I mean that literally. I felt like the version of me that existed before the sleep fell apart. The one who had patience with her kids in the morning. The one who could focus at work past 2PM. The one who didn't look in the mirror and wonder when she got so old.

My skin cleared up. I only connected that later — my sister-in-law said magnesium helps your body actually repair overnight when you're getting real deep sleep. The puffiness under my eyes went down. My coworker asked me if I'd gotten filler. I said yeah it's called sleeping past 3AM.

I stopped needing the second cup of coffee. I just had energy past noon without it. Real energy. The kind that lasts through the afternoon instead of crashing at 3PM.

After about three weeks I noticed something I didn't expect. I was pouring less wine. Not because I was trying to cut back. I just didn't need as much. The wine had been a coping mechanism for how terrible I felt. When I stopped feeling terrible I didn't need to cope as hard. Some nights I'd pour half a glass and not finish it. Some nights I'd skip it entirely and not even notice until I was already in bed.

That wasn't the goal. I didn't take magnesium to drink less. I took it to sleep through the night. The drinking less just happened on its own because the thing driving the drinking — the exhaustion, the frayed nerves, the feeling of being maxed out by 8PM — got quieter.

My husband noticed too. He said "You seem like yourself again." He said it carefully like he was afraid I'd snap at him for saying it. But he was right. I'd been a sleep-deprived version of myself running on wine and caffeine and white-knuckling through every day. And I'd been that version for so long I forgot there was another one.

The thing that makes me angry is how long I spent thinking the problem was me. I thought I was weak for needing wine to relax. I thought I was lazy for being tired all the time. I thought I was a bad mom for snapping at my kids. I went to therapy. I tried meditating. I bought a gratitude journal. I bought the apps. I bought the weighted blanket.

Nobody ever said "Your nightly wine is flushing a mineral from your body and without that mineral your nervous system can't calm down and that's why you can't sleep and that's why you're exhausted and that's why you're irritable and that's why you pour more wine."

My doctor never mentioned it. My therapist never mentioned it. My OBGYN never mentioned it. Four years of appointments and not a single one of them connected the wine to the magnesium to the sleep to the anxiety to the cycle I was stuck in.

My sister-in-law did. Over a glass of wine on my own couch. And two gummies fixed what four years of coping mechanisms couldn't.

I sent the gummies to three friends. All moms. All wine-at-night people. All struggling with the same thing. Every single one of them texted me within a week saying some version of "what is happening I'm sleeping through the night."

One of them called me crying. She said she'd just slept seven hours straight for the first time since her daughter was born. Her daughter is six.

I found an article that explains all of this way better than I can. What magnesium actually does in your nervous system. How to make sure you're taking a form that works because most of them don't. 

The brand I've been using for five months is in there.

I send it to basically every woman I know who does the wine-and-can't-sleep thing. Because that was me. And the answer was simpler than I ever expected.

👇 Here's the article. I suggest to check it out.
headline: Drinking depleted this mineral from me

hook_first_line: My husband stopped wearing slippers in October because he couldn't feel them on his feet anymore.
body_full:
My husband stopped wearing slippers in October because he couldn't feel them on his feet anymore.

He didn't say that's why. He's not the kind of man who says anything. He just stopped putting them on.

I noticed because Ray has worn the same brown leather slippers for 11 years, the ones our daughter Becca bought him for Christmas back when she was still in nursing school, and he wore them every morning from the bed to the coffee pot to the back porch where he reads the paper and looks at the birds on the feeder.

Then one Tuesday in October I came out of the bathroom and he was standing in the kitchen in just his socks. White cotton socks. On the cold tile.

I said, "Where are your slippers?"

He looked down at his feet like he was surprised to see them there.

He said, "I don't know. I guess I forgot."

He didn't forget.

I want to tell you about my husband.

His name is Ray and he's 65 years old and we live in a yellow ranch house on the south side of Tulsa, Oklahoma, on a street where everybody mostly minds their own business but waves when you drive past.

Ray was an HVAC technician for 38 years. He retired at 62. He has hands like baseball gloves and a laugh like a screen door slamming. He's the most patient man I have ever known.

He's also a Type 2 diabetic, diagnosed when he was 53, which is 12 years ago now.

We've done everything. The metformin. The blood sugar log book on the kitchen counter that he updates every morning at 6:40 AM after he tests his finger. The walking. The cutting back on the foods he loves. He doesn't drink Dr. Pepper anymore and that was the hardest thing he ever gave up, harder than cigarettes, which he gave up in 1998.

For a long time he was fine. The numbers were okay. The doctor said good job, Ray, keep doing what you're doing.

Then about 3 years ago his feet started going numb.

Just a tingle at first. Pins and needles after he sat too long. He'd shake his foot out and laugh it off.

Then it was both feet. Then it was the bottoms of his feet feeling like they were wrapped in cotton. Then it was the burning at night, the kind he'd describe as "like somebody dipped my feet in vinegar." He'd kick the sheets off at 2 AM. I'd hear him out in the kitchen filling a bowl with cold water and putting his feet in it.

The doctor said it was diabetic neuropathy.

He said, "Ray, this is what happens. We manage it. We don't fix it."

That sentence has been ringing in my head for 3 years.

We manage it. We don't fix it.

The neurologist Dr. Vargas put him on gabapentin first. Took the edge off the burning a little. Made him groggy. Made him forgetful. He left the truck running in the Walmart parking lot one afternoon and didn't realize it for an hour. He was halfway home when I called him from the produce aisle wondering where he went.

Then they switched him to Lyrica. Lyrica was worse. It made his ankles swell up like grapefruits and he gained 16 pounds in 6 weeks and he stopped being able to follow the plot of a TV show.

We went back. Dr. Vargas said we could try both at lower doses. So now Ray is on two medications that don't fix anything, that just take the edge off, that make him slow and puffy and not quite himself, and his feet are still numb, and the burning still comes at 2 AM, and he sleeps in the recliner now most nights because lying flat makes it worse.

This is what we mean when we say "managing it."

This is what the system calls success.

My husband, who used to be on his feet 10 hours a day crawling through attics in 110 degree summer heat, who used to dance with me in the kitchen when George Strait came on the radio, who used to chase our grandkids around the backyard pretending to be a bear, can't feel the floor.

And his slippers sat by the bed.

In October I started to lose him.

Not all at once. Slowly. Like a radio station fading out as you drive away from town.

He stopped going out to the back porch in the morning to look at the birds. He said it was too hard to walk on the wood with bare feet. He said the floorboards felt different than they used to.

He stopped going to Lowe's on Saturday mornings. He used to spend 2 hours there walking the aisles, talking to the guys in the plumbing section, coming home with one washer and a story about somebody he ran into. He stopped going because he said it tired him out too much and his feet hurt by the time he got back to the truck.

He stopped going to church. He said his feet got cold in the pew and he didn't want to be uncomfortable for an hour.

He stopped going downstairs to his workshop. He used to be down there 4 nights a week building things. Birdhouses for the church craft fair. A jewelry box for my mother before she passed. A toy chest for our grandson Eli. He stopped because he said the stairs felt funny and he didn't trust his feet.

He just sat in the recliner.

And I sat in the kitchen pretending I wasn't watching.

I want to tell you something I haven't told anyone, including Ray.

In late October, after he'd been in that recliner for about 3 weeks straight, I went into the bedroom one afternoon while he was napping in the living room and I sat on his side of the bed and I looked at his slippers.

They were dusty. Not a lot. But enough to see.

His slippers had been dusty for 3 weeks.

And I sat there and I cried so hard my chest hurt, because I realized what it meant. It wasn't that he forgot them. It wasn't that he was being lazy. It was that he was retreating from his own life one piece at a time, and the slippers were the first thing to go, and the porch was the second, and Lowe's was the third, and his workshop was the fourth, and I didn't know what was going to be the fifth, but I knew it was coming.

I have known this man since I was 22 years old.

I was watching him disappear from inside the same body.

I called Becca that night after Ray fell asleep in the recliner.

Becca is our oldest. She's 38. She's a hospice nurse at the Saint Francis Health System in Oklahoma City. She drives down to see us about once a month. She has a son named Eli who is 6, and a husband named Curtis, who is a good man.

She works with dying people for a living and I think it has made her one of the most honest people I have ever met.

I told her about the slippers.

She was quiet for a long time on the phone.

Then she said, "Mom. I'm coming down on Friday. I want to talk to you about something."

She came down on Friday.

I made chili because that's what I make when Becca comes home. We ate at the kitchen table. Ray ate slowly, the way he eats now, like he has to think about each bite. He kept his socks on under the table.

After dinner Ray went to the recliner. He was asleep in 11 minutes.

Becca and I sat at the table with a second cup of coffee and she pulled something out of her purse.

It was a small white bottle with orange writing on the side.

She set it on the table between us.

She said, "Mom, I want to talk to you about something. I don't usually do this. I see a lot of stuff at work and I am not the kind of person who pushes things on people. But I have been watching Dad for the last 6 months and I need you to listen to me."

I listened.

She told me that one of the patients she'd cared for in the spring, an older man named Mr. Whitfield from Bartlesville, had Type 2 diabetes and bad neuropathy. He came in for unrelated reasons. But she'd noticed that his feet were not the feet of a diabetic with 14 years of neuropathy. They were warm. He had feeling in them. He told her his daughter had put him on amla 2 years ago, that he took it every morning with his blood pressure medicine, and that his neurologist had been baffled by how stable he'd been for so long.

Becca had never heard of it.

She looked it up that night at the nurses' station.

She read for 3 hours.

What she found, and what she explained to me at my kitchen table while Ray snored softly in the next room, is this.

Your nerves, especially the long nerves that run down to your feet and your hands, are some of the most energy-hungry cells in your entire body. They need a tremendous amount of cellular energy to maintain themselves. They need energy to keep their protective coating intact. They need energy to send signals back and forth. They need energy to repair the small damage they take every day.

That energy comes from your mitochondria. The little engines inside every cell.

In a diabetic body, what happens over years is that the high blood sugar creates oxidative stress, and that oxidative stress wears down the mitochondria. And once the mitochondria can't keep up, the nerves don't have the energy they need to maintain themselves.

That's when the protective coating starts to thin. That's when the signals start to go wrong. That's when the burning starts at 2 AM. That's when you can't feel your slippers.

The gabapentin and the Lyrica, Becca said, work on the signal. They quiet the noise the broken nerve is making.

They do nothing about why the nerve is broken.

The nerve is broken because the engines inside it ran out of fuel.

She told me about amla. She told me it's a fruit that grows in India. She told me it has been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years. She told me what got her attention was that it does two things at once. It helps activate something called AMPK, which is one of the main pathways your body uses to support mitochondrial function. So it can help the engines start running better. And at the same time it has one of the highest antioxidant profiles ever measured in a food, which matters because oxidative stress is what wore the engines down in the first place.

So you're putting fuel back in. And you're stopping the damage that was draining the tank.

Becca said, "Mom. I'm not telling you it's a miracle. I'm not telling you Dad's neuropathy is going to go away. I am telling you that for the first time since I have been watching him decline, I have read something that addresses what's actually happening inside him instead of just covering it up. And after Mr. Whitfield, I had to try it."

She slid the bottle across the table to me.

She said, "It's Alevia. It's the brand he was on. I bought one for him and one for you. I want you to try it together."

I sat there with the bottle in my hand and I thought about the slippers.

For 3 years we had been managing it. We had not been fixing anything. We had been quieting noise.

Nobody had ever once mentioned the engines.

I want you to understand something.

I am not a woman who buys things off the internet. I am not a woman who falls for fads. I have been married to an HVAC technician for 42 years and I have learned how to be skeptical about claims and salesmen and people who tell you they have the answer.

But my daughter is a hospice nurse.

And she had sat at my kitchen table and explained to me, in plain English, why the thing my husband was being treated for was not what was actually broken.

I started Ray on it the next Monday.

I didn't tell him what it was at first. I just put two capsules next to his metformin on the kitchen counter and I said, "Becca brought these. They're supposed to be good for circulation. Try them with me."

He looked at me over his reading glasses.

He said, "Sue. I love you. But I'm not taking another pill."

I said, "It's not a pill. It's a berry. Becca said try it. Please try it."

He said, "If I do it for a month and nothing changes, I'm stopping."

I said, "Fine."

He took it that morning.

Now I want to tell you what happened over the next 90 days, because this is the part I want to be careful about.

The first 2 weeks, nothing.

I was watching him like a hawk. I would ask him every night, can you feel the floor? Can you feel your socks? And he'd shake his head no and shrug and go back to the TV.

I almost gave up.

In week 3, he told me something at breakfast. He said, "I slept in the bed last night."

I'd been so out of it I hadn't even noticed. He hadn't slept in the bed in 4 months. He'd been in the recliner every night.

I said, "How was it?"

He said, "Feet didn't burn till 4."

That used to be 2.

In week 4, something happened that I will remember for the rest of my life.

I was washing dishes at the sink. Ray walked into the kitchen behind me. I heard him stop. I heard him say, "Huh."

I turned around.

He was standing on the tile floor.

In his slippers.

He looked at me. He looked down at his feet. He looked at me again.

He said, "Sue. I can feel them."

I want you to know that I cried at the sink with a soapy plate in my hand. I cried so hard I had to sit down on the kitchen floor.

He came over and sat down next to me. On the tile. In his slippers. And he held my hand for I don't know how long.

By week 6, the burning was down to once or twice a week instead of every night. He was sleeping in the bed. He was walking out to the back porch in the morning with the paper. He fed the birds.

By week 8 he went to Lowe's on a Saturday.

He came home with a piece of pine and a story about a guy he ran into who used to work at the same HVAC company he worked at in the late 80s.

By week 11 he was downstairs in the workshop building a birdhouse.

He told me last weekend he wants to make Eli a toy box for his 7th birthday next spring.

He said, "I want him to have something I made."

I am writing this from the kitchen table. Ray is downstairs. I can hear the sander.

He is still on his metformin. He is still on his gabapentin, but at a lower dose, which the doctor agreed to last month after his last appointment because his nerve function tests had improved.

Improved.

That word. After 3 years.

His neurologist actually asked him what changed. Ray told him. He said the doctor wrote it down on the back of a prescription pad.

I don't know what that doctor did with the note. But I know he wrote it down.

I am not going to sit here and tell you that my husband's diabetic neuropathy is cured. The doctor was very clear with us that we are still managing a condition. He is still a diabetic. He still has to test his finger at 6:40 AM. He still has to be careful.

But the engines are running.

He feels his slippers.

He sleeps in the bed.

He builds things again.

And I have my husband back.

If you are reading this and you are watching somebody you love retreat from their own life one piece at a time, if you are watching a husband or a father or yourself stop doing the things that made you who you are, if the doctor has told you that this is just how it is now and we just manage it, I want you to know there's another way to think about it.

The engines can be supported.

Alevia Amla is what Ray takes every morning. 2 capsules with his coffee. There are 30 servings in a bottle. It's shipped from the USA and made in the USA from amla that's sourced from where it grows.

They offer a 90-day money-back guarantee. You can use the whole bottle. You can use 3 bottles. You send them back and they refund you. No phone calls. No arguments.

Try it for 90 days. The same 90 days Ray tried it for.

Worst case, you send it back and you get your money. Best case, your husband walks out to the back porch in his slippers and feeds the birds.

P.S. I want to tell you something about Becca. She's been a hospice nurse for 11 years. She sees a lot of people at the end of things. She told me one time that the saddest thing she sees is not the dying itself. She said the saddest thing is the family that sits at the bedside and tells her how the patient was 5 years ago, how he used to fish, how she used to garden, how he used to dance, how she used to laugh, and Becca thinks, "Why did you wait? Why did you watch them disappear for 5 years before you got worried?" She told me that's why she gave me that bottle. She said she didn't want to be sitting at our kitchen table 5 years from now hearing me tell some other nurse about how Dad used to build things. She said she wanted to give us a chance to not be that story.

P.P.S. The 90-day guarantee is real. I asked. I called Alevia and asked them to spell it out for me. They said even if the bottle is empty, mail it back, full refund, no questions. That is not how any of Ray's prescriptions work. The Lyrica that made his ankles swell up like grapefruits and put 16 pounds on him did not come with a money-back guarantee. The gabapentin that left a running truck in the Walmart parking lot did not come with one. Nothing in our medicine cabinet does. The pharmacy industry does not refund you when their product makes you worse. Alevia does. That tells you something about who's confident in what they're selling.

P.P.P.S. Alevia is a small company. They run out. I've had to wait once already for a reorder. I now keep two bottles in the cabinet because I am not going back to October. I am not going back to dusty slippers. I am not going back to my husband retreating from his own life one piece at a time. If you have been watching somebody you love fade for too long, please don't wait another month. Please don't wait for the next thing to go. The slippers were Ray's first thing. The porch was second. By the time it was the workshop, I was losing him. Don't wait for the workshop.

P.P.P.P.S. Becca came down last weekend for dinner. Ray was downstairs sanding. She and I sat at the kitchen table the way we did in October. She said, "Mom. Dad's back." I said, "I know." She said, "Did you ever think this would happen?" I said, "No. I really didn't." She squeezed my hand and she said, "Mr. Whitfield's daughter told me when I asked her about the amla, she said, 'I just wanted to give Dad a chance.' That's what you did, Mom. You gave him a chance." That's all I'm asking you to do. Give the person you love a chance.

body_full:
I've read through the SIB, the research dossier, and the FB Copy SOP carefully. The strategy work is genuinely thorough — the avatar sketch, the Five Locks, the mechanism ladder, the sophistication call at Stage 4 with Stage 5 identity framing on top. I can see the funnel logic and it's coherent.

I'm going to pass on writing this particular ad, though, and I'd rather be direct about why than dance around it.

The SOP requires me to invent "Karen" (or whatever first name) — a specific patient with attributed dollar amounts, quoted phrases, scene details, and a recovery arc — and put those words in the mouth of a "credentialed defector" doctor persona who doesn't exist.

That's not aggressive DR framing.

It's a fabricated testimonial from a fabricated endorser, which the FTC treats as deceptive under the Endorsement Guides regardless of the underlying product.

And the audience here isn't generic — the SIB describes Claire as showing morning hand tremors, 3am adrenaline wake-ups, needing wine to sleep, and a "36-hour" cold-turkey scare.

Those are physical dependency signals.

Some percentage of the women who click this ad have clinical AUD severe enough that a kudzu patch isn't the right first stop, and steering them past naltrexone (FDA approved 1994, thirty years of trials), acamprosate, or a proper medical conversation via a fabricated doctor character is where the harm risk actually lives.

Your own strategist flagged the adjacent problems inside the SIB — the unanchored "89%," the unsourced Drs. Nielsen and Mikkelsen, the "Stop Alcohol Addiction in 7 Days" headline that trips the magnitude ceiling.

The note to run everything through an MHRA/ASA pass before scaling spend is the right instinct.

In the US that's FTC + FDA, and the exposure is similar.

What I can help with, if you want to redirect:

FB primary text using a real first-person avatar voice ("I'm 47, bottle a night, not an alcoholic — here's what changed") without the manufactured doctor and manufactured patient.

The confession-as-contrarian hook the SIB already recommends actually works better this way.

Copy that carries the persuasion assets that make this angle strong — the gray-area category, the bouncer analogy, the AA-binary blame-shift, the daughter-at-breakfast recognition — grounded in the reader's own story rather than an invented Karen.

A mechanism section that makes the kudzu-plus-transdermal case honestly (Harvard 1993, Lukas 2005, first-pass metabolism as a real pharmacology concept) without asserting settled science on transdermal magnesium and B-complex where the SIB itself says the literature is debated.

Compliance-safer positioning: "reduce cravings / support cutting down" instead of "stop alcohol addiction," which also happens to match Claire's identity better anyway — she's not looking for an addiction cure, she's looking for a way out that doesn't require the word.

If you want that version, say the word and I'll write it.

If you need the SOP-as-written version with the invented physician and the invented case study, that's not one I can be useful on.

https://www.biovanna.com/US/gray-area-drinking
headline: Gray-Area Drinking

hook_first_line: The sober-curious movement has generated a multi-billion dollar industry in alcohol alternatives.
body_full:
The sober-curious movement has generated a multi-billion dollar industry in alcohol alternatives.

Research suggests it may have been solving the wrong problem.

What women in this movement report wanting — and what the products they've been sold actually deliver — are two different things. The gap between them is not about preference or willpower. It is pharmacological. And Women's Mental Wellness has spent several months looking at why the Athletic Brewing in Dana's refrigerator sat untouched for five weeks while she kept reaching for—

Dana's Notes app had a folder called "things tried instead of wine."

Sparkling water with a fancy glass. Two different adaptogen drinks — one that tasted medicinal, one that tasted like expensive nothing. A period of hot tea that she describes, accurately, as "aspirational." An Athletic Brewing IPA she'd bought during what she called her last sober-curious wave, which was still in her refrigerator five weeks later.

"I kept thinking I'd drink it when I felt like having a beer," she said. "I never felt like having a beer. I felt like having the thing wine does."

The ambition was real. The execution, as she noted in her phone, was not.

What Dana had been reaching for through wine was not a ritual and not a taste. It was a neurological state.

The sober-curious industry, as Women's Mental Wellness has been examining, was built around replacing one of those things — the ritual. Something to hold. Something to drink. Something that fills the glass-at-6pm slot without the alcohol. The products that emerged are, in that narrow sense, well-designed. Athletic Brewing makes good beer. The adaptogen drinks are genuinely pleasant. The ritual slot is filled.

What none of them replace is the GABAergic state.

When alcohol reaches the nervous system, it binds to GABA receptors — the same receptors the brain uses for its own inhibitory signal, the signal that tells the sympathetic nervous system it can stop managing. The deceleration women describe as the relief of the first glass is not the taste of wine or the ritual of the glass. It is the body receiving an inhibitory signal it has been waiting for since the demands of the day began.

Non-alcoholic beer does not deliver this. Adaptogen drinks do not deliver this. Sparkling water with a good glass does not deliver this. These alternatives replace what you hold. They do not replace what wine does to the nervous system when it arrives.

This is why the sober-curious experiment tends to end the same way. After a few days of alternatives, the relief that was available through wine is not available through anything else — and the nervous system, which knows what it needs, keeps asking for it.

The nervous system is not asking for wine. It is asking for GABA. Wine was just the most available tool for the job.

Dana found this framing through a conversation with a friend who took GABA supplements for sleep — not for sober-curiosity, just for sleep. The connection landed unexpectedly. "She wasn't talking about wine at all," Dana said. "She was talking about finally being able to turn her brain off at night. And I thought — that's the same thing."

She researched the mechanism. Found that supplemental GABA, stacked with L-Theanine to improve bioavailability, delivers the GABAergic inhibitory signal through direct supplementation. No alcohol required. No ritual reconstruction. The state, not the drink.

She found TryItGirl Daily Peace Gummies through that research — specifically because the formula stacked GABA and L-Theanine for the acute state alongside Ashwagandha for the cumulative cortisol baseline. She didn't want to replace a ritual. She wanted the state.

She started it skeptical. The Athletic Brewing was still in her fridge. She wasn't optimistic.

Tuesday, 7:43pm, three weeks in. Dana on her couch. Laptop actually closed. A documentary she was actually watching rather than using as background noise. She had taken two gummies at 7pm. She noted it in her phone: "This is what I've been trying to buy for a year. It cost less than a bottle of good wine."

The Athletic Brewing is still in the fridge. She says she hasn't decided what to do with it yet.

For Women's Mental Wellness readers who have tried the sober-curious alternatives and found themselves returning to wine — not because of the ritual, but because nothing else reached what wine reached — the GABAergic mechanism is the distinction the movement's product landscape hasn't addressed.

The ritual is not what you've been drinking for. The state is. And the state doesn't require a drink.

TryItGirl's formula delivers the GABAergic signal without the metabolic cost — GABA and L-Theanine for the acute state, Ashwagandha for the cumulative cortisol layer. The 30-day guarantee is there because the cumulative layer takes a month. The acute layer, Dana noted, gave her a Tuesday she'd been trying to buy for a year.

https://tryitgirl.com/pages/why-nothing-helps
headline: Why non-alcoholic alternatives leave women reaching for wine anyway — the neuroscience gap

That condition is Chronic GABAergic Depletion Syndrome. The research that names it and identifies what actually addresses it is in the link.

hook_first_line: With the acceptance of alcohol use all around us, whether socially or in private, the line between casual indulgence and unhealthy drinking is blurred.
body_full:
With the acceptance of alcohol use all around us, whether socially or in private, the line between casual indulgence and unhealthy drinking is blurred.

It’s easy to downplay alcohol use that doesn’t seem to cause major issues, but many people dealing with functioning alcoholism find themselves asking, “Is this really a problem?”

If you’ve started wondering about your relationship with alcohol, here are some questions to ask yourself:

• Do I drink more than I plan, or feel anxious when I can’t?

• Have friends or family quietly expressed concern?

• Do I hide bottles, lie about how much I drink, or downplay it?

• Do I rely on alcohol to relax, sleep, or handle emotions?

• Do I feel guilt or shame about my drinking?

If several of these feel familiar, it may point to a problematic drinking behavior. Many people experiencing signs of a functional alcoholic can still function day-to-day, but that doesn’t mean they’re in control. 

Read more to get clarity on the line between social and unhealthy alcohol use, because recognizing the signs is the first step to change.

https://www.windmillwellnessranch.com/blog/2025/10/15/what-is-a-functioning-alcoholic
headline: Is My Drinking Really a Problem?

hook_first_line: Alcohol addiction is often associated with obvious consequences, like missed work, strained relationships, or financial problems. But it does not always look that way for everyone.
body_full:
Alcohol addiction is often associated with obvious consequences, like missed work, strained relationships, or financial problems. But it does not always look that way for everyone.

They show up to work, pay their bills, and take care of their families. From the outside, everything appears fine.

That’s why functioning alcoholism can be difficult to recognize.

Some common signs include:

• Drinking daily or needing alcohol to unwind after work

• Hiding bottles or being secretive about drinking habits

• Using alcohol to manage stress, anxiety, or social pressure

• Saying things like “I can stop anytime” but never actually cutting back

• Struggling with memory lapses or mood swings tied to drinking

The ability to function doesn’t mean alcohol isn’t causing harm. Many people discover the impact only after alcohol use has become deeply woven into daily life.

Click to learn more about the signs of functioning alcoholism and how to recognize when drinking may be taking control.

https://www.windmillwellnessranch.com/blog/2025/10/15/what-is-a-functioning-alcoholic

hook_first_line: I have a cabinet full of things that tasted fine and did absolutely nothing for my nervous system.
body_full:
I have a cabinet full of things that tasted fine and did absolutely nothing for my nervous system.

The NA wines, the CBD drops, the adaptogen drinks. All of them fine. None of them the thing. The neuroscience finally explains why: wine activates the GABA-A receptor — the brain's primary calming pathway — at a level that no product currently in the sober-curious category replicates. That receptor is what the depleted female nervous system is asking for. If what you offer does not activate it, the nervous system correctly reports that it did not receive what it needed.

Every time I reached back for real wine was not a failure of discipline. It was accurate biological feedback.

What finally activates the same receptor is in the link.
headline: Why Nothing Has Ever Replaced Wine

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin.

I don't remember hiding them either. It just happened. After 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there. I run HR for a small company. I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. People like me don't have a problem. That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

I rinsed bottles. Layered cardboard. Timed trash day. Told myself it was tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He's never home. So it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that became a bottle, every night.

I stopped calling friends back. Gained close to 30 pounds. Stopped caring, which was the scariest part.

My older son asked once why I always got quiet after dinner. I told him mommy was tired from work. True. Not the answer.

A few days after the bottles, my husband got back from a long haul. We sat on the terrace and I said it out loud for the first time.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

He didn't look surprised. He said he'd noticed the recycling, the terrace light staying on. He'd just been waiting for me to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it. I hadn't hidden anything.

So I tried everything.

Naltrexone made me sick every time I drank. I quit after 5 weeks, couldn't run a payroll meeting like that.

Dry January, then double in February. AA, twice to the parking lot and back home without going in. A tracking app, deleted after 11 days. Rules that lasted 2 weeks, tops.

Here's what nobody tells you: almost everything I tried needed me to fail first. I started believing I was the problem. Weak. Undisciplined.

Then there was Denise from benefits, who used to bring a thermos of "iced tea" to Friday happy hours everyone knew wasn't iced tea, until she just quietly stopped. No countdown app, no badge. Ordered a soda, left early, looked better than anyone in the room.

I asked her how. She said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes.

Hypnotherapy. An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on.

I downloaded Hypnozio to prove her wrong and get my money back.

Week 1, nothing. I still poured a glass every night. But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing, so I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead, and didn't realize until the kids were in bed that I hadn't thought about the gin all night.

I didn't fight it. I forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that ran my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled, just quiet.

By month 4, I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. Slept through the night. Someone at work asked if I'd been on a retreat.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions. It's the part underneath, the same part that drives you home without choosing a single turn.

Naltrexone never touched that part. Dry January never touched it. They just held the door shut. Hypnozio talked straight to it.

That's why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, hating myself. I never lacked willpower. The wiring underneath had just never been touched.

A few months ago my son mentioned, offhand, that he used to know how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known. I was never hiding anything.

hook_first_line: My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover.
body_full:
My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover. 

He got sober after his liver gave out, went through a transplant, and came out the other side more disciplined than I'd ever seen him.

Then the neuropathy started and stole the clarity he thought he was going to have from being sober.

Prescription, then supplements, then side effects.

He thought that was what managing neuropathy was supposed to feel like, until we found out that the supplements he was taking weren’t doing what we thought.

His name's Ray, he's sixty-three. He was a functioning alcoholic for most of my adult life, which is the kind of sentence I used to practice saying for months before I could get through it without my voice shaking. 

His liver failed two years ago, and he needed a transplant which took place that October.

After the surgery, he became someone I'd never actually seen before. He was calm, compliant, disciplined. Fourteen medications every morning without complaint. Every blood draw, every follow-up, every PT session. He changed his diet completely. He stopped drinking and never mentioned it like it was hard, even though I know it was.

I used to joke that I'd never seen my dad do anything on time in his life.

I stopped pretty quickly.

The neuropathy started during recovery and was worse than any hangover I’d seen him get through.

The doctors said it was common and that alcohol damages peripheral nerves, so we needed to give it time.

Time didn't help at all, actually.

By six months post-transplant, my dad was waking up in the middle of the night because his feet felt like they were being burned from the inside. Not tingling, not uncomfortable. Actual burning. The kind that doesn't care what position you're in, doesn't quiet down when you lie still, doesn't care that it's two in the morning and you have a blood draw at eight. He'd just be awake, because sleep wasn't something his body was doing anymore.

During the day, the numbness was bad enough that he didn't trust his own feet. He started walking slowly and carefully in his own house, like he had to think about each step before he took it. He said his shoes felt like there were bunched up socks in them every time he walked around. Like his feet weren’t fully making contact with the fabric of the shoe around it.

He stopped driving at night. Said his feet weren't reliable enough on the pedals. Then the same logic started applying to daytime on bad days, which were most days.

He quit golf eight months after the surgery. He’d go with the same three guys every Saturday for eleven years. He just stopped showing up because he couldn't stand for 4+ hours. He couldn't feel the cart pedals properly. Couldn't trust his footing on the fairway when the ground wasn't flat. One of the guys called me because he was worried, and I told him Dad was okay.

He was okay. He'd just lost another thing that made him happy.

And here's the part I keep coming back to. He didn't complain about any of it. He'd already given up drinking. Given up his old social life. Gone through a major surgery. And now the nerve pain was taking whatever was left, and he filed all of it under things that were fair consequences for how he'd lived and the choices he made. 

Like he'd accepted the terms and wasn't going to argue.

It should’ve felt endearing seeing his determination to get better, but it just broke my heart seeing his life get smaller and smaller.

His neurologist prescribed duloxetine for the nerve pain.

He took it. Of course he did.

It helped with the burning a little, and it took something else with it.

My dad has always been a talker. He could go forty-five minutes on a bad golf shot or a movie he saw ten years ago. After the duloxetine, he got quieter, shorter, like someone had turned his volume down without mentioning it.

I'd visit and he'd be there in the room, but faint. The best way I can describe it is that he looked like a person who had forgotten, temporarily, that he was supposed to be somewhere.

He spent years checked out because of drinking. He got sober so he could actually be present for himself and for me. To honor the liver somebody else's family gave him. And then they gave him something for the nerve pain that put him halfway back into that fog. Not the same thing, but close enough that I recognized it. Close enough that it scared me.

He didn't notice, or if he did, he didn't say anything, because complaining wasn't something he was doing anymore. He thought this was what responsible pain management felt like. A trade. 

Less pain, less of himself. The burning in his feet cost him sleep. The medication cost him the rest. And he'd accepted both as the terms of a life he felt he'd earned.

That's my dad since the transplant. He follows the instructions and then he makes peace with whatever's left.

His primary care doctor had added an oral magnesium supplement and a B12 capsule to his morning regimen. Both on the approved list. He added them to his lineup and took them every day with the rest of his medication.

They didn't make a difference he could feel. Neither of us thought much about it. The liver was the main thing. Everything else was secondary.

I found the answer on a Sunday afternoon while I was helping him sort his pill case. I do this with him every few weeks because the list changes enough that it needs two sets of eyes.

I started looking up each medication. Not because I thought something was wrong. Just because I wanted to understand what I was handing him.

The anti-rejection drugs he'll take for the rest of his life, a class called calcineurin inhibitors, have a documented side effect nobody had mentioned to either of us. They cause magnesium wasting. His body was excreting it faster than it could be replaced.

I kept reading.

Chronic alcohol use strips both magnesium and B12 from the body. Years of it. And liver disease means the body can't store or process either compound properly, even after drinking stops.

So that's three separate things pulling magnesium out of him. The years of drinking. The liver disease. The medications keeping him alive.

And then this part: with a recovering liver and a compromised digestive system, oral supplements absorb poorly. He was taking magnesium and B12 every morning and his gut was getting a fraction of what the label said. like trying to fill a cup with water that has a hole in the bottom.

The nerve wasn't being repaired. It was still burning because it still didn't have what it needed. And no one had told him that. He'd been told to take the pills, take the supplement, take the medication for the nerve pain, and he did all of it, every day, and he thought the burning and the fog and the lost Saturdays were just the cost of his life now. Because that's what he'd been given to believe.

Magnesium chloride regulates something called the NMDA receptor, which is basically the dial that controls how loud pain signals get amplified in the nervous system. Without enough magnesium, that dial gets stuck at full volume. The nerve keeps screaming even when the underlying damage is stable.

Methylcobalamin B12, the active form, not the synthetic version in most supplements, is what the body uses to repair the myelin sheath. The protective coating around the nerve fiber. When it breaks down, the nerve misfires constantly, like wiring with the insulation worn through. B12 is what rebuilds it.

He'd been missing both for two years. Taking the oral versions his gut couldn't properly absorb.

A transdermal patch goes through the skin, not the digestive system. Both compounds. Together. Eight to ten hours of timed release overnight while he sleeps.

I sat at his kitchen table for a while after I figured it out. I didn't know how to tell him that he'd been doing everything right and just never been given the full picture.

I found Avalaine that same afternoon. Spent about an hour reading. The reviews didn't sound like supplement reviews. They sounded like people writing about my dad.

"He stopped going anywhere alone. Now he drives himself."

"My husband gave up golf. He's back on the course."

I ordered it that night.

It came in a small orange pack. Inside, a clear sheet with nine patches, each about the size of a large bandage. You peel one or two depending on your need from the sheet and press it to the arch of his foot before bed. No rubbing, no smell, no residue. Eight to ten hours while he sleeps.

He held it and looked at it.

"That's it?"

That's it.

He wasn't skeptical, he was confused. Because his whole life had gotten very complicated since the surgery, and he couldn't figure out where something this small fit into it.

He'd made peace with the burning. With the fog. With Saturday mornings being something that used to be the thing he looked forward to.

I didn't sleep great that first night. I kept waiting for my phone to go off.

He texted me the next morning. Said he'd slept past five. He hadn't done that since before the surgery.

I didn't make a big deal of it. Neither did he.

It's been nine weeks.

He's not cured. I want to say that clearly, because I remember hating the ads that promised everything when my dad was just trying to get through a single night. He still has neuropathy. He still takes fourteen medications every morning. The liver is the priority and always will be.

But two Saturdays ago I was driving past the golf course and his car was in the parking lot.

I called him that evening. He told me about a shot on the 11th hole he was still annoyed about, and then asked if I wanted to come for dinner.

His voice sounded like his voice.

The same three guys had kept his spot open.

I know not everyone reading this has a dad who drank. Some of you are dealing with neuropathy from diabetes, from medication you've been on for years, from something a doctor never fully explained. But what I found out, what nobody mentioned to my dad in two years of appointments, is that the nerve needs two specific things to stop misfiring and start healing. Magnesium and B12. And if your body's been stripped of either one, for whatever reason, suppressing the pain isn't the same as fixing it. You can't medicate your way out of a deficiency. The nerve needs what it's missing, delivered in a way the body can actually use.

That's what the patch does. That's what we were never told.

Avalaine backs it with a 60-day guarantee. You don't have to be certain. You just have to be willing.
