His primary care doctor had added an oral magnesium supplement and a B12 capsule to his morning regimen. Both on the approved list. He added them to his lineup and took them every day with the rest of his medication.

They didn't make a difference he could feel. Neither of us thought much about it. The liver was the main thing. Everything else was secondary.

I found the answer on a Sunday afternoon while I was helping him sort his pill case. I do this with him every few weeks because the list changes enough that it needs two sets of eyes.

I started looking up each medication. Not because I thought something was wrong. Just because I wanted to understand what I was handing him.

The anti-rejection drugs he'll take for the rest of his life, a class called calcineurin inhibitors, have a documented side effect nobody had mentioned to either of us. They cause magnesium wasting. His body was excreting it faster than it could be replaced.

I kept reading.

Chronic alcohol use strips both magnesium and B12 from the body. Years of it. And liver disease means the body can't store or process either compound properly, even after drinking stops.

So that's three separate things pulling magnesium out of him. The years of drinking. The liver disease. The medications keeping him alive.

And then this part: with a recovering liver and a compromised digestive system, oral supplements absorb poorly. He was taking magnesium and B12 every morning and his gut was getting a fraction of what the label said. like trying to fill a cup with water that has a hole in the bottom.

The nerve wasn't being repaired. It was still burning because it still didn't have what it needed. And no one had told him that. He'd been told to take the pills, take the supplement, take the medication for the nerve pain, and he did all of it, every day, and he thought the burning and the fog and the lost Saturdays were just the cost of his life now. Because that's what he'd been given to believe.

Magnesium chloride regulates something called the NMDA receptor, which is basically the dial that controls how loud pain signals get amplified in the nervous system. Without enough magnesium, that dial gets stuck at full volume. The nerve keeps screaming even when the underlying damage is stable.

Methylcobalamin B12, the active form, not the synthetic version in most supplements, is what the body uses to repair the myelin sheath. The protective coating around the nerve fiber. When it breaks down, the nerve misfires constantly, like wiring with the insulation worn through. B12 is what rebuilds it.

He'd been missing both for two years. Taking the oral versions his gut couldn't properly absorb.

A transdermal patch goes through the skin, not the digestive system. Both compounds. Together. Eight to ten hours of timed release overnight while he sleeps.

I sat at his kitchen table for a while after I figured it out. I didn't know how to tell him that he'd been doing everything right and just never been given the full picture.

I found Avalaine that same afternoon. Spent about an hour reading. The reviews didn't sound like supplement reviews. They sounded like people writing about my dad.

"He stopped going anywhere alone. Now he drives himself."

"My husband gave up golf. He's back on the course."

I ordered it that night.

It came in a small orange pack. Inside, a clear sheet with nine patches, each about the size of a large bandage. You peel one or two depending on your need from the sheet and press it to the arch of his foot before bed. No rubbing, no smell, no residue. Eight to ten hours while he sleeps.

He held it and looked at it.

"That's it?"

That's it.

He wasn't skeptical, he was confused. Because his whole life had gotten very complicated since the surgery, and he couldn't figure out where something this small fit into it.

He'd made peace with the burning. With the fog. With Saturday mornings being something that used to be the thing he looked forward to.

I didn't sleep great that first night. I kept waiting for my phone to go off.

He texted me the next morning. Said he'd slept past five. He hadn't done that since before the surgery.

I didn't make a big deal of it. Neither did he.

It's been nine weeks.

He's not cured. I want to say that clearly, because I remember hating the ads that promised everything when my dad was just trying to get through a single night. He still has neuropathy. He still takes fourteen medications every morning. The liver is the priority and always will be.

But two Saturdays ago I was driving past the golf course and his car was in the parking lot.

I called him that evening. He told me about a shot on the 11th hole he was still annoyed about, and then asked if I wanted to come for dinner.

His voice sounded like his voice.

The same three guys had kept his spot open.

I know not everyone reading this has a dad who drank. Some of you are dealing with neuropathy from diabetes, from medication you've been on for years, from something a doctor never fully explained. But what I found out, what nobody mentioned to my dad in two years of appointments, is that the nerve needs two specific things to stop misfiring and start healing. Magnesium and B12. And if your body's been stripped of either one, for whatever reason, suppressing the pain isn't the same as fixing it. You can't medicate your way out of a deficiency. The nerve needs what it's missing, delivered in a way the body can actually use.

That's what the patch does. That's what we were never told.

Avalaine backs it with a 60-day guarantee. You don't have to be certain. You just have to be willing.

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin.

I don't remember hiding them either. It just happened. After 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there. I run HR for a small company. I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. People like me don't have a problem. That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

I rinsed bottles. Layered cardboard. Timed trash day. Told myself it was tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He's never home. So it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that became a bottle, every night.

I stopped calling friends back. Gained close to 30 pounds. Stopped caring, which was the scariest part.

My older son asked once why I always got quiet after dinner. I told him mommy was tired from work. True. Not the answer.

A few days after the bottles, my husband got back from a long haul. We sat on the terrace and I said it out loud for the first time.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

He didn't look surprised. He said he'd noticed the recycling, the terrace light staying on. He'd just been waiting for me to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it. I hadn't hidden anything.

So I tried everything.

Naltrexone made me sick every time I drank. I quit after 5 weeks, couldn't run a payroll meeting like that.

Dry January, then double in February. AA, twice to the parking lot and back home without going in. A tracking app, deleted after 11 days. Rules that lasted 2 weeks, tops.

Here's what nobody tells you: almost everything I tried needed me to fail first. I started believing I was the problem. Weak. Undisciplined.

Then there was Denise from benefits, who used to bring a thermos of "iced tea" to Friday happy hours everyone knew wasn't iced tea, until she just quietly stopped. No countdown app, no badge. Ordered a soda, left early, looked better than anyone in the room.

I asked her how. She said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes.

Hypnotherapy. An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on.

I downloaded Hypnozio to prove her wrong and get my money back.

Week 1, nothing. I still poured a glass every night. But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing, so I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead, and didn't realize until the kids were in bed that I hadn't thought about the gin all night.

I didn't fight it. I forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that ran my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled, just quiet.

By month 4, I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. Slept through the night. Someone at work asked if I'd been on a retreat.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions. It's the part underneath, the same part that drives you home without choosing a single turn.

Naltrexone never touched that part. Dry January never touched it. They just held the door shut. Hypnozio talked straight to it.

That's why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, hating myself. I never lacked willpower. The wiring underneath had just never been touched.

A few months ago my son mentioned, offhand, that he used to know how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known. I was never hiding anything.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero. No pills, no meetings, no white-knuckling.

I sleep through the night. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and watch the sunset instead of drinking through it. When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked, because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin. It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck: you're not broken. It's not your fault. Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

I used this program: https://hypnozio.com/landing-alc?psc=checkout-148a-alc&l=en&vndr=hypfbalcch3nocoreen
headline: It's not willpower. It's a loop.

hook_first_line: For over 20 years, my daily medicine was four to five drinks. Every single day.
body_full:
For over 20 years, my daily medicine was four to five drinks. Every single day.

I was what they call a "high-functioning alcoholic." That’s a dangerous term, because it makes you think you’re getting away with it. Only a very few people close to me knew the truth. On the outside, I looked like a success. I was in the corporate world, constantly entertaining clients. The routine was always the same: take them out to a nice steak dinner, have a couple of drinks. Take them to the bar afterward, have a couple more.

It was just "business." Until it wasn't.

The brain fog started rolling in. I couldn't remember things. I'd sit there and think, Man, is this what I've become? Is this the best I'm ever going to be? My wife had been begging me to quit for a really long time, but I just wasn't ready. I was too deep in the cycle.

Then, one night, lying in bed, something just clicked. I rolled over, looked at my beautiful wife, and said, "I think I'm done drinking."

She almost fell out of bed.

I didn't do a 12-step program, but I was smart about it. I researched and found out you can literally kill yourself quitting cold turkey after 20 years. So I went to a doctor the very next day, got medicine for the withdrawals, and stopped. Just like that.

It was the best decision of my entire life. The fog lifted. My brain works again. My body functions the way it’s supposed to. I didn't even realize how miserable and out of shape I was until I finally got free.

hook_first_line: With the acceptance of alcohol use all around us, whether socially or in private, the line between casual indulgence and unhealthy drinking is blurred.
body_full:
With the acceptance of alcohol use all around us, whether socially or in private, the line between casual indulgence and unhealthy drinking is blurred.

It’s easy to downplay alcohol use that doesn’t seem to cause major issues, but many people dealing with functioning alcoholism find themselves asking, “Is this really a problem?”

If you’ve started wondering about your relationship with alcohol, here are some questions to ask yourself:

• Do I drink more than I plan, or feel anxious when I can’t?

• Have friends or family quietly expressed concern?

• Do I hide bottles, lie about how much I drink, or downplay it?

• Do I rely on alcohol to relax, sleep, or handle emotions?

• Do I feel guilt or shame about my drinking?

If several of these feel familiar, it may point to a problematic drinking behavior. Many people experiencing signs of a functional alcoholic can still function day-to-day, but that doesn’t mean they’re in control. 

Read more to get clarity on the line between social and unhealthy alcohol use, because recognizing the signs is the first step to change.

https://www.windmillwellnessranch.com/blog/2025/10/15/what-is-a-functioning-alcoholic

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin.

I don't remember hiding them either. It just happened. After 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there. I run HR for a small company. I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. People like me don't have a problem. That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

I rinsed bottles. Layered cardboard. Timed trash day. Told myself it was tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He's never home. So it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that became a bottle, every night.

I stopped calling friends back. Gained close to 30 pounds. Stopped caring, which was the scariest part.

My older son asked once why I always got quiet after dinner. I told him mommy was tired from work. True. Not the answer.

A few days after the bottles, my husband got back from a long haul. We sat on the terrace and I said it out loud for the first time.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

He didn't look surprised. He said he'd noticed the recycling, the terrace light staying on. He'd just been waiting for me to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it. I hadn't hidden anything.

So I tried everything.

Naltrexone made me sick every time I drank. I quit after 5 weeks, couldn't run a payroll meeting like that.

Dry January, then double in February. AA, twice to the parking lot and back home without going in. A tracking app, deleted after 11 days. Rules that lasted 2 weeks, tops.

Here's what nobody tells you: almost everything I tried needed me to fail first. I started believing I was the problem. Weak. Undisciplined.

Then there was Denise from benefits, who used to bring a thermos of "iced tea" to Friday happy hours everyone knew wasn't iced tea, until she just quietly stopped. No countdown app, no badge. Ordered a soda, left early, looked better than anyone in the room.

I asked her how. She said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes.

Hypnotherapy. An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on.

I downloaded Hypnozio to prove her wrong and get my money back.

Week 1, nothing. I still poured a glass every night. But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing, so I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead, and didn't realize until the kids were in bed that I hadn't thought about the gin all night.

I didn't fight it. I forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that ran my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled, just quiet.

By month 4, I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. Slept through the night. Someone at work asked if I'd been on a retreat.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions. It's the part underneath, the same part that drives you home without choosing a single turn.

Naltrexone never touched that part. Dry January never touched it. They just held the door shut. Hypnozio talked straight to it.

That's why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, hating myself. I never lacked willpower. The wiring underneath had just never been touched.

A few months ago my son mentioned, offhand, that he used to know how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known. I was never hiding anything.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero. No pills, no meetings, no white-knuckling.

I sleep through the night. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and watch the sunset instead of drinking through it. When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked, because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin. It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck: you're not broken. It's not your fault. Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

I have never in my life wanted to take words back more than I wanted to take those back. And I couldn't even remember saying them.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin. I'd been timing trash day around how full it looked.

I don't remember deciding to hide them either. It just happened. The way habits do after 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there.

I run HR for a small local company. I handle other people's problems for a living.

I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I was never the falling-down kind. Never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. Never showed up to a meeting with liquor on my breath.

I had a mortgage. 2 kids. A title with my name on the org chart.

People like me don't have a problem.

That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

By the time my husband found those bottles, I'd been rinsing and stacking for over 2 of them. Layering cardboard on top so a quick glance wouldn't show how many. Timing trash day around how full it looked.

I told myself that was just tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He loves me and the kids. He's just never home.

So most nights it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that used to be wine and became gin, and became more gin. I watched my own life go by like it belonged to somebody else.

I stopped calling my friends back. I gained close to 30 pounds in 3 years. My skin changed. My hair changed.

And the scariest part wasn't any of that.

It was that I didn't care.

Most nights when he called from the road, I don't remember what we talked about. The nights I do remember, I remember him going quiet in a certain way. Careful. Like he already suspected something and didn't want to be right.

My older son asked me once why I always got quiet after dinner.

I told him mommy was tired from work.

That was true. It wasn't the answer.

The night that changed things wasn't dramatic. It was a Sunday, a few days after the bottles.

My husband had just gotten back from a long haul. The kids were asleep. We sat where I always sat, on the terrace, and I said it out loud for the first time in my life.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

I was shaking when I said it.

He didn't look surprised.

He told me he'd been worried for a long time. That he'd noticed the recycling. That he'd noticed the terrace light on long after the kids were down. He'd just been waiting for me to be the one to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it.

I hadn't hidden anything.

I couldn't think about anything else for weeks.

So I tried everything. I decided I'd rather get scammed 9 times than sit still once.

Naltrexone first. My husband was supportive, so we tried it together. Now I know exactly how those pills work. You don't want the drink because the drink makes you sick. Nauseous. Dizzy. Headaches that lasted into the afternoon.

I couldn't run a payroll meeting like that. I stopped after 5 weeks.

Dry January. I white-knuckled all 31 days and drank double in February, like I owed myself something.

AA. I drove to the church twice. Both times I sat in the parking lot and never opened the car door. I'd already said the word once, out loud, to my husband. I couldn't say it to a room of strangers.

Tracking apps. I counted drinks like calories for 11 days and deleted it.

Rules. Only wine. Only weekends. Only after the kids were down. Every rule lost eventually, usually within 2 weeks.

Here's what nobody tells you. Almost everything I tried needed me to fail before it could work. The rules reset when I broke them. Naltrexone only worked while I was actively suffering. Dry January was just a countdown to February.

I started to believe I was the problem. Not the drinking. Me. Weak. Undisciplined. One of those people who just can't do it.

Then there was Denise.

Denise runs our benefits program. For years she brought a thermos of "iced tea" to our Friday happy hours that everyone quietly knew wasn't iced tea.

Then, over a few months, she just stopped. Not loudly. No countdown app. No badge. At our holiday happy hour this year she ordered a soda, had half of it, and left early to pick up her kids.

She looked better than anyone in the room.

I watched her leave that soda on the table, still half full, and felt something close to grief.

When I finally asked her how, she said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes so hard it hurt.

Hypnotherapy.

An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on. Cheaper than the gin I'd bought that morning.

I'm not a spiritual person. I calculate PTO accrual for a living. My whole personality is a spreadsheet.

So I downloaded Hypnozio for exactly 1 reason. To prove Denise wrong, use it for a week, and ask for my money back.

Week 1, nothing happened. I still poured a glass every night. I almost deleted it.

But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing. So I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead and sat on the terrace, and it wasn't until the kids were in bed that I realized I hadn't thought about the gin once all night.

I didn't fight it. I just forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that had run my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled. Not resisted. Quiet.

If you've ever fought a craving you know the difference. Fighting one is loud. It takes up your whole body.

This was just absence.

By month 4 I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. My skin came back. I slept through the night for the first time since my youngest was born. Someone at work asked if I'd been away on a retreat.

I started reading about why it worked, and it was the first explanation in 3 years that made sense of my own life.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions.

It's the part underneath. The one on autopilot.

The same part that drives you all the way home without you consciously choosing a single turn.

That's the part every pill and every countdown and every rule ignores. They talk to the conscious you. They hand you rules.

But the part that pours the glass never got the memo.

Which is exactly why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, in a dark kitchen, hating myself.

It was never that I lacked willpower.

The wiring underneath was just never touched.

A few months ago, my son said something offhand while we were taking out the trash together. He said he used to be able to tell how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known.

For years I thought I was hiding it under that cardboard. I wasn't hiding anything.

That conversation sat with me longer than the one on the terrace did.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero.

No pills. No meetings. No white-knuckling a day count.

I sleep through the night. The weight is almost gone. My skin and my hair came back. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and actually watch the sunset instead of drinking through it.

When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked. Because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin.

It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck, hear me.

You're not broken. It's not your fault.

You've been fighting the wrong battle this whole time.

Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

hook_first_line: “I didn’t hit rock bottom. I didn’t lose my job.
body_full:
“I didn’t hit rock bottom. I didn’t lose my job.

But every single morning at 3:17 AM, staring at the ceiling with my heart hammering in my chest... I knew something had to change.” 😣👇

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Let’s be honest.

In our fast-paced world, that "one glass of wine to take the edge off" after a stressful workday can sneak up on you so quickly.

Before I knew it, pouring a drink at 6 PM became an automatic reflex.

I hated what came next:
❌ The constant brain fog every morning
❌ The sluggish, exhausted afternoons
❌ And worst of all... the crushing 'hanxiety'

That awful wave of anxiety, panic, and guilt that floods your mind at 3 AM when the rest of the world is asleep.

The absolute turning point came when I looked at my 12-year-old daughter. She was giving me that cautious look—checking to see "which version of Mom" she got today.

My heart completely broke. I knew I couldn’t keep living like this.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

I tried everything to cut back:

Willpower? Lasted about 4 days before a stressful day wiped it out.
Prescription meds? Made me violently nauseous and dizzy.
AA meetings? Felt like branding myself as "broken." I didn't want to feel powerless... I just wanted to be normal.

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin.

I don't remember hiding them either. It just happened. After 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there. I run HR for a small company. I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. People like me don't have a problem. That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

I rinsed bottles. Layered cardboard. Timed trash day. Told myself it was tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He's never home. So it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that became a bottle, every night.

I stopped calling friends back. Gained close to 30 pounds. Stopped caring, which was the scariest part.

My older son asked once why I always got quiet after dinner. I told him mommy was tired from work. True. Not the answer.

A few days after the bottles, my husband got back from a long haul. We sat on the terrace and I said it out loud for the first time.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

He didn't look surprised. He said he'd noticed the recycling, the terrace light staying on. He'd just been waiting for me to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it. I hadn't hidden anything.

So I tried everything.

Naltrexone made me sick every time I drank. I quit after 5 weeks, couldn't run a payroll meeting like that.

Dry January, then double in February. AA, twice to the parking lot and back home without going in. A tracking app, deleted after 11 days. Rules that lasted 2 weeks, tops.

Here's what nobody tells you: almost everything I tried needed me to fail first. I started believing I was the problem. Weak. Undisciplined.

Then there was Denise from benefits, who used to bring a thermos of "iced tea" to Friday happy hours everyone knew wasn't iced tea, until she just quietly stopped. No countdown app, no badge. Ordered a soda, left early, looked better than anyone in the room.

I asked her how. She said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes.

Hypnotherapy. An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on.

I downloaded Hypnozio to prove her wrong and get my money back.

Week 1, nothing. I still poured a glass every night. But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing, so I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead, and didn't realize until the kids were in bed that I hadn't thought about the gin all night.

I didn't fight it. I forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that ran my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled, just quiet.

By month 4, I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. Slept through the night. Someone at work asked if I'd been on a retreat.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions. It's the part underneath, the same part that drives you home without choosing a single turn.

Naltrexone never touched that part. Dry January never touched it. They just held the door shut. Hypnozio talked straight to it.

That's why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, hating myself. I never lacked willpower. The wiring underneath had just never been touched.

A few months ago my son mentioned, offhand, that he used to know how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known. I was never hiding anything.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero. No pills, no meetings, no white-knuckling.

I sleep through the night. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and watch the sunset instead of drinking through it. When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked, because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin. It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck: you're not broken. It's not your fault. Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

hook_first_line: My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover.
body_full:
My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover. 

He got sober after his liver gave out, went through a transplant, and came out the other side more disciplined than I'd ever seen him.

Then the neuropathy started and stole the clarity he thought he was going to have from being sober.

Prescription, then supplements, then side effects.

He thought that was what managing neuropathy was supposed to feel like, until we found out that the supplements he was taking weren’t doing what we thought.

His name's Ray, he's sixty-three. He was a functioning alcoholic for most of my adult life, which is the kind of sentence I used to practice saying for months before I could get through it without my voice shaking. 

His liver failed two years ago, and he needed a transplant which took place that October.

After the surgery, he became someone I'd never actually seen before. He was calm, compliant, disciplined. Fourteen medications every morning without complaint. Every blood draw, every follow-up, every PT session. He changed his diet completely. He stopped drinking and never mentioned it like it was hard, even though I know it was.

I used to joke that I'd never seen my dad do anything on time in his life.

I stopped pretty quickly.

The neuropathy started during recovery and was worse than any hangover I’d seen him get through.

The doctors said it was common and that alcohol damages peripheral nerves, so we needed to give it time.

Time didn't help at all, actually.

By six months post-transplant, my dad was waking up in the middle of the night because his feet felt like they were being burned from the inside. Not tingling, not uncomfortable. Actual burning. The kind that doesn't care what position you're in, doesn't quiet down when you lie still, doesn't care that it's two in the morning and you have a blood draw at eight. He'd just be awake, because sleep wasn't something his body was doing anymore.

During the day, the numbness was bad enough that he didn't trust his own feet. He started walking slowly and carefully in his own house, like he had to think about each step before he took it. He said his shoes felt like there were bunched up socks in them every time he walked around. Like his feet weren’t fully making contact with the fabric of the shoe around it.

He stopped driving at night. Said his feet weren't reliable enough on the pedals. Then the same logic started applying to daytime on bad days, which were most days.

He quit golf eight months after the surgery. He’d go with the same three guys every Saturday for eleven years. He just stopped showing up because he couldn't stand for 4+ hours. He couldn't feel the cart pedals properly. Couldn't trust his footing on the fairway when the ground wasn't flat. One of the guys called me because he was worried, and I told him Dad was okay.

He was okay. He'd just lost another thing that made him happy.

And here's the part I keep coming back to. He didn't complain about any of it. He'd already given up drinking. Given up his old social life. Gone through a major surgery. And now the nerve pain was taking whatever was left, and he filed all of it under things that were fair consequences for how he'd lived and the choices he made. 

Like he'd accepted the terms and wasn't going to argue.

It should’ve felt endearing seeing his determination to get better, but it just broke my heart seeing his life get smaller and smaller.

His neurologist prescribed duloxetine for the nerve pain.

He took it. Of course he did.

It helped with the burning a little, and it took something else with it.

My dad has always been a talker. He could go forty-five minutes on a bad golf shot or a movie he saw ten years ago. After the duloxetine, he got quieter, shorter, like someone had turned his volume down without mentioning it.

I'd visit and he'd be there in the room, but faint. The best way I can describe it is that he looked like a person who had forgotten, temporarily, that he was supposed to be somewhere.

He spent years checked out because of drinking. He got sober so he could actually be present for himself and for me. To honor the liver somebody else's family gave him. And then they gave him something for the nerve pain that put him halfway back into that fog. Not the same thing, but close enough that I recognized it. Close enough that it scared me.

He didn't notice, or if he did, he didn't say anything, because complaining wasn't something he was doing anymore. He thought this was what responsible pain management felt like. A trade. 

Less pain, less of himself. The burning in his feet cost him sleep. The medication cost him the rest. And he'd accepted both as the terms of a life he felt he'd earned.

That's my dad since the transplant. He follows the instructions and then he makes peace with whatever's left.

His primary care doctor had added an oral magnesium supplement and a B12 capsule to his morning regimen. Both on the approved list. He added them to his lineup and took them every day with the rest of his medication.

They didn't make a difference he could feel. Neither of us thought much about it. The liver was the main thing. Everything else was secondary.

I found the answer on a Sunday afternoon while I was helping him sort his pill case. I do this with him every few weeks because the list changes enough that it needs two sets of eyes.

I started looking up each medication. Not because I thought something was wrong. Just because I wanted to understand what I was handing him.

The anti-rejection drugs he'll take for the rest of his life, a class called calcineurin inhibitors, have a documented side effect nobody had mentioned to either of us. They cause magnesium wasting. His body was excreting it faster than it could be replaced.

I kept reading.

Chronic alcohol use strips both magnesium and B12 from the body. Years of it. And liver disease means the body can't store or process either compound properly, even after drinking stops.

So that's three separate things pulling magnesium out of him. The years of drinking. The liver disease. The medications keeping him alive.

And then this part: with a recovering liver and a compromised digestive system, oral supplements absorb poorly. He was taking magnesium and B12 every morning and his gut was getting a fraction of what the label said. like trying to fill a cup with water that has a hole in the bottom.

The nerve wasn't being repaired. It was still burning because it still didn't have what it needed. And no one had told him that. He'd been told to take the pills, take the supplement, take the medication for the nerve pain, and he did all of it, every day, and he thought the burning and the fog and the lost Saturdays were just the cost of his life now. Because that's what he'd been given to believe.

Magnesium chloride regulates something called the NMDA receptor, which is basically the dial that controls how loud pain signals get amplified in the nervous system. Without enough magnesium, that dial gets stuck at full volume. The nerve keeps screaming even when the underlying damage is stable.

Methylcobalamin B12, the active form, not the synthetic version in most supplements, is what the body uses to repair the myelin sheath. The protective coating around the nerve fiber. When it breaks down, the nerve misfires constantly, like wiring with the insulation worn through. B12 is what rebuilds it.

He'd been missing both for two years. Taking the oral versions his gut couldn't properly absorb.

A transdermal patch goes through the skin, not the digestive system. Both compounds. Together. Eight to ten hours of timed release overnight while he sleeps.

I sat at his kitchen table for a while after I figured it out. I didn't know how to tell him that he'd been doing everything right and just never been given the full picture.

I found Avalaine that same afternoon. Spent about an hour reading. The reviews didn't sound like supplement reviews. They sounded like people writing about my dad.

"He stopped going anywhere alone. Now he drives himself."

"My husband gave up golf. He's back on the course."

I ordered it that night.

It came in a small orange pack. Inside, a clear sheet with nine patches, each about the size of a large bandage. You peel one or two depending on your need from the sheet and press it to the arch of his foot before bed. No rubbing, no smell, no residue. Eight to ten hours while he sleeps.

He held it and looked at it.

"That's it?"

That's it.

He wasn't skeptical, he was confused. Because his whole life had gotten very complicated since the surgery, and he couldn't figure out where something this small fit into it.

He'd made peace with the burning. With the fog. With Saturday mornings being something that used to be the thing he looked forward to.

I didn't sleep great that first night. I kept waiting for my phone to go off.

He texted me the next morning. Said he'd slept past five. He hadn't done that since before the surgery.

I didn't make a big deal of it. Neither did he.

It's been nine weeks.

He's not cured. I want to say that clearly, because I remember hating the ads that promised everything when my dad was just trying to get through a single night. He still has neuropathy. He still takes fourteen medications every morning. The liver is the priority and always will be.

But two Saturdays ago I was driving past the golf course and his car was in the parking lot.

I called him that evening. He told me about a shot on the 11th hole he was still annoyed about, and then asked if I wanted to come for dinner.

His voice sounded like his voice.

The same three guys had kept his spot open.

I know not everyone reading this has a dad who drank. Some of you are dealing with neuropathy from diabetes, from medication you've been on for years, from something a doctor never fully explained. But what I found out, what nobody mentioned to my dad in two years of appointments, is that the nerve needs two specific things to stop misfiring and start healing. Magnesium and B12. And if your body's been stripped of either one, for whatever reason, suppressing the pain isn't the same as fixing it. You can't medicate your way out of a deficiency. The nerve needs what it's missing, delivered in a way the body can actually use.

That's what the patch does. That's what we were never told.

Avalaine backs it with a 60-day guarantee. You don't have to be certain. You just have to be willing.

hook_first_line: I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.
body_full:
I was so drunk that night I don't remember hanging up on my husband mid-sentence.

He told me the next morning what I'd said before the line went dead: that I wished he'd just stay on the road forever so I could drink in peace.

2 days later, he found 11 empty bottles rinsed and stacked under the cardboard in our recycling bin.

I don't remember hiding them either. It just happened. After 3 years of practice.

I'm a functioning alcoholic.

I go to work. I stay sober there. I run HR for a small company. I take care of my kids.

And every night, alone on the terrace, I drank until I stopped feeling anything.

I never missed a shift. Never got pulled over. People like me don't have a problem. That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

I rinsed bottles. Layered cardboard. Timed trash day. Told myself it was tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He's never home. So it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that became a bottle, every night.

I stopped calling friends back. Gained close to 30 pounds. Stopped caring, which was the scariest part.

My older son asked once why I always got quiet after dinner. I told him mommy was tired from work. True. Not the answer.

A few days after the bottles, my husband got back from a long haul. We sat on the terrace and I said it out loud for the first time.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

He didn't look surprised. He said he'd noticed the recycling, the terrace light staying on. He'd just been waiting for me to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it. I hadn't hidden anything.

So I tried everything.

Naltrexone made me sick every time I drank. I quit after 5 weeks, couldn't run a payroll meeting like that.

Dry January, then double in February. AA, twice to the parking lot and back home without going in. A tracking app, deleted after 11 days. Rules that lasted 2 weeks, tops.

Here's what nobody tells you: almost everything I tried needed me to fail first. I started believing I was the problem. Weak. Undisciplined.

Then there was Denise from benefits, who used to bring a thermos of "iced tea" to Friday happy hours everyone knew wasn't iced tea, until she just quietly stopped. No countdown app, no badge. Ordered a soda, left early, looked better than anyone in the room.

I asked her how. She said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes.

Hypnotherapy. An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on.

I downloaded Hypnozio to prove her wrong and get my money back.

Week 1, nothing. I still poured a glass every night. But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing, so I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead, and didn't realize until the kids were in bed that I hadn't thought about the gin all night.

I didn't fight it. I forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that ran my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled, just quiet.

By month 4, I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. Slept through the night. Someone at work asked if I'd been on a retreat.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions. It's the part underneath, the same part that drives you home without choosing a single turn.

Naltrexone never touched that part. Dry January never touched it. They just held the door shut. Hypnozio talked straight to it.

That's why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, hating myself. I never lacked willpower. The wiring underneath had just never been touched.

A few months ago my son mentioned, offhand, that he used to know how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known. I was never hiding anything.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero. No pills, no meetings, no white-knuckling.

I sleep through the night. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and watch the sunset instead of drinking through it. When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked, because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin. It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck: you're not broken. It's not your fault. Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

hook_first_line: My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover.
body_full:
My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover. 

He got sober after his liver gave out, went through a transplant, and came out the other side more disciplined than I'd ever seen him.

Then the neuropathy started and stole the clarity he thought he was going to have from being sober.

Prescription, then supplements, then side effects.

He thought that was what managing neuropathy was supposed to feel like, until we found out that the supplements he was taking weren’t doing what we thought.

His name's Ray, he's sixty-three. He was a functioning alcoholic for most of my adult life, which is the kind of sentence I used to practice saying for months before I could get through it without my voice shaking. 

His liver failed two years ago, and he needed a transplant which took place that October.

After the surgery, he became someone I'd never actually seen before. He was calm, compliant, disciplined. Fourteen medications every morning without complaint. Every blood draw, every follow-up, every PT session. He changed his diet completely. He stopped drinking and never mentioned it like it was hard, even though I know it was.

I used to joke that I'd never seen my dad do anything on time in his life.

I stopped pretty quickly.

The neuropathy started during recovery and was worse than any hangover I’d seen him get through.

The doctors said it was common and that alcohol damages peripheral nerves, so we needed to give it time.

Time didn't help at all, actually.

By six months post-transplant, my dad was waking up in the middle of the night because his feet felt like they were being burned from the inside. Not tingling, not uncomfortable. Actual burning. The kind that doesn't care what position you're in, doesn't quiet down when you lie still, doesn't care that it's two in the morning and you have a blood draw at eight. He'd just be awake, because sleep wasn't something his body was doing anymore.

During the day, the numbness was bad enough that he didn't trust his own feet. He started walking slowly and carefully in his own house, like he had to think about each step before he took it. He said his shoes felt like there were bunched up socks in them every time he walked around. Like his feet weren’t fully making contact with the fabric of the shoe around it.

He stopped driving at night. Said his feet weren't reliable enough on the pedals. Then the same logic started applying to daytime on bad days, which were most days.

He quit golf eight months after the surgery. He’d go with the same three guys every Saturday for eleven years. He just stopped showing up because he couldn't stand for 4+ hours. He couldn't feel the cart pedals properly. Couldn't trust his footing on the fairway when the ground wasn't flat. One of the guys called me because he was worried, and I told him Dad was okay.

He was okay. He'd just lost another thing that made him happy.

And here's the part I keep coming back to. He didn't complain about any of it. He'd already given up drinking. Given up his old social life. Gone through a major surgery. And now the nerve pain was taking whatever was left, and he filed all of it under things that were fair consequences for how he'd lived and the choices he made. 

Like he'd accepted the terms and wasn't going to argue.

It should’ve felt endearing seeing his determination to get better, but it just broke my heart seeing his life get smaller and smaller.

His neurologist prescribed duloxetine for the nerve pain.

He took it. Of course he did.

It helped with the burning a little, and it took something else with it.

My dad has always been a talker. He could go forty-five minutes on a bad golf shot or a movie he saw ten years ago. After the duloxetine, he got quieter, shorter, like someone had turned his volume down without mentioning it.

I'd visit and he'd be there in the room, but faint. The best way I can describe it is that he looked like a person who had forgotten, temporarily, that he was supposed to be somewhere.

He spent years checked out because of drinking. He got sober so he could actually be present for himself and for me. To honor the liver somebody else's family gave him. And then they gave him something for the nerve pain that put him halfway back into that fog. Not the same thing, but close enough that I recognized it. Close enough that it scared me.

He didn't notice, or if he did, he didn't say anything, because complaining wasn't something he was doing anymore. He thought this was what responsible pain management felt like. A trade. 

Less pain, less of himself. The burning in his feet cost him sleep. The medication cost him the rest. And he'd accepted both as the terms of a life he felt he'd earned.

That's my dad since the transplant. He follows the instructions and then he makes peace with whatever's left.

His primary care doctor had added an oral magnesium supplement and a B12 capsule to his morning regimen. Both on the approved list. He added them to his lineup and took them every day with the rest of his medication.

They didn't make a difference he could feel. Neither of us thought much about it. The liver was the main thing. Everything else was secondary.

I found the answer on a Sunday afternoon while I was helping him sort his pill case. I do this with him every few weeks because the list changes enough that it needs two sets of eyes.

I started looking up each medication. Not because I thought something was wrong. Just because I wanted to understand what I was handing him.

The anti-rejection drugs he'll take for the rest of his life, a class called calcineurin inhibitors, have a documented side effect nobody had mentioned to either of us. They cause magnesium wasting. His body was excreting it faster than it could be replaced.

I kept reading.

Chronic alcohol use strips both magnesium and B12 from the body. Years of it. And liver disease means the body can't store or process either compound properly, even after drinking stops.

So that's three separate things pulling magnesium out of him. The years of drinking. The liver disease. The medications keeping him alive.

And then this part: with a recovering liver and a compromised digestive system, oral supplements absorb poorly. He was taking magnesium and B12 every morning and his gut was getting a fraction of what the label said. like trying to fill a cup with water that has a hole in the bottom.

The nerve wasn't being repaired. It was still burning because it still didn't have what it needed. And no one had told him that. He'd been told to take the pills, take the supplement, take the medication for the nerve pain, and he did all of it, every day, and he thought the burning and the fog and the lost Saturdays were just the cost of his life now. Because that's what he'd been given to believe.

Magnesium chloride regulates something called the NMDA receptor, which is basically the dial that controls how loud pain signals get amplified in the nervous system. Without enough magnesium, that dial gets stuck at full volume. The nerve keeps screaming even when the underlying damage is stable.

Methylcobalamin B12, the active form, not the synthetic version in most supplements, is what the body uses to repair the myelin sheath. The protective coating around the nerve fiber. When it breaks down, the nerve misfires constantly, like wiring with the insulation worn through. B12 is what rebuilds it.

He'd been missing both for two years. Taking the oral versions his gut couldn't properly absorb.

A transdermal patch goes through the skin, not the digestive system. Both compounds. Together. Eight to ten hours of timed release overnight while he sleeps.

I sat at his kitchen table for a while after I figured it out. I didn't know how to tell him that he'd been doing everything right and just never been given the full picture.

I found Avalaine that same afternoon. Spent about an hour reading. The reviews didn't sound like supplement reviews. They sounded like people writing about my dad.

"He stopped going anywhere alone. Now he drives himself."

"My husband gave up golf. He's back on the course."

I ordered it that night.

It came in a small orange pack. Inside, a clear sheet with nine patches, each about the size of a large bandage. You peel one or two depending on your need from the sheet and press it to the arch of his foot before bed. No rubbing, no smell, no residue. Eight to ten hours while he sleeps.

He held it and looked at it.

"That's it?"

That's it.

He wasn't skeptical, he was confused. Because his whole life had gotten very complicated since the surgery, and he couldn't figure out where something this small fit into it.

He'd made peace with the burning. With the fog. With Saturday mornings being something that used to be the thing he looked forward to.

I didn't sleep great that first night. I kept waiting for my phone to go off.

He texted me the next morning. Said he'd slept past five. He hadn't done that since before the surgery.

I didn't make a big deal of it. Neither did he.

It's been nine weeks.

He's not cured. I want to say that clearly, because I remember hating the ads that promised everything when my dad was just trying to get through a single night. He still has neuropathy. He still takes fourteen medications every morning. The liver is the priority and always will be.

But two Saturdays ago I was driving past the golf course and his car was in the parking lot.

I called him that evening. He told me about a shot on the 11th hole he was still annoyed about, and then asked if I wanted to come for dinner.

His voice sounded like his voice.

The same three guys had kept his spot open.

I know not everyone reading this has a dad who drank. Some of you are dealing with neuropathy from diabetes, from medication you've been on for years, from something a doctor never fully explained. But what I found out, what nobody mentioned to my dad in two years of appointments, is that the nerve needs two specific things to stop misfiring and start healing. Magnesium and B12. And if your body's been stripped of either one, for whatever reason, suppressing the pain isn't the same as fixing it. You can't medicate your way out of a deficiency. The nerve needs what it's missing, delivered in a way the body can actually use.

That's what the patch does. That's what we were never told.

Avalaine backs it with a 60-day guarantee. You don't have to be certain. You just have to be willing.

I had a mortgage. 2 kids. A title with my name on the org chart.

People like me don't have a problem.

That was the story I lived in for 3 years.

By the time my husband found those bottles, I'd been rinsing and stacking for over 2 of them. Layering cardboard on top so a quick glance wouldn't show how many. Timing trash day around how full it looked.

I told myself that was just tidiness.

Nobody rinses bottles like that for tidiness.

My husband drives long-haul. He loves me and the kids. He's just never home.

So most nights it was just me, the terrace, and a glass that used to be wine and became gin, and became more gin. I watched my own life go by like it belonged to somebody else.

I stopped calling my friends back. I gained close to 30 pounds in 3 years. My skin changed. My hair changed.

And the scariest part wasn't any of that.

It was that I didn't care.

Most nights when he called from the road, I don't remember what we talked about. The nights I do remember, I remember him going quiet in a certain way. Careful. Like he already suspected something and didn't want to be right.

My older son asked me once why I always got quiet after dinner.

I told him mommy was tired from work.

That was true. It wasn't the answer.

The night that changed things wasn't dramatic. It was a Sunday, a few days after the bottles.

My husband had just gotten back from a long haul. The kids were asleep. We sat where I always sat, on the terrace, and I said it out loud for the first time in my life.

I have a problem. I need to stop.

I was shaking when I said it.

He didn't look surprised.

He told me he'd been worried for a long time. That he'd noticed the recycling. That he'd noticed the terrace light on long after the kids were down. He'd just been waiting for me to be the one to say it.

I thought I'd been hiding it.

I hadn't hidden anything.

I couldn't think about anything else for weeks.

So I tried everything. I decided I'd rather get scammed 9 times than sit still once.

Naltrexone first. My husband was supportive, so we tried it together. Now I know exactly how those pills work. You don't want the drink because the drink makes you sick. Nauseous. Dizzy. Headaches that lasted into the afternoon.

I couldn't run a payroll meeting like that. I stopped after 5 weeks.

Dry January. I white-knuckled all 31 days and drank double in February, like I owed myself something.

AA. I drove to the church twice. Both times I sat in the parking lot and never opened the car door. I'd already said the word once, out loud, to my husband. I couldn't say it to a room of strangers.

Tracking apps. I counted drinks like calories for 11 days and deleted it.

I didn't fight it. I just forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that had run my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled. Not resisted. Quiet.

If you've ever fought a craving you know the difference. Fighting one is loud. It takes up your whole body.

This was just absence.

By month 4 I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. My skin came back. I slept through the night for the first time since my youngest was born. Someone at work asked if I'd been away on a retreat.

I started reading about why it worked, and it was the first explanation in 3 years that made sense of my own life.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions.

It's the part underneath. The one on autopilot.

The same part that drives you all the way home without you consciously choosing a single turn.

That's the part every pill and every countdown and every rule ignores. They talk to the conscious you. They hand you rules.

But the part that pours the glass never got the memo.

Which is exactly why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, in a dark kitchen, hating myself.

It was never that I lacked willpower.

The wiring underneath was just never touched.

He'd known. My kids had known.

For years I thought I was hiding it under that cardboard. I wasn't hiding anything.

That conversation sat with me longer than the one on the terrace did.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero.

No pills. No meetings. No white-knuckling a day count.

I sleep through the night. The weight is almost gone. My skin and my hair came back. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and actually watch the sunset instead of drinking through it.

When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked. Because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin.

It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck, hear me.

You're not broken. It's not your fault.

You've been fighting the wrong battle this whole time.

Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.

hook_first_line: My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover.
body_full:
My dad spent years being hammered most of the day, then waking up to a head-splitting hangover.
He got sober after his liver gave out, went through a transplant, and came out the other side more disciplined than I'd ever seen him.
Then the neuropathy started and stole the clarity he thought he was going to have from being sober.
Prescription, then supplements, then side effects.
He thought that was what managing neuropathy was supposed to feel like, until we found out the supplement he was taking every morning was never aimed at the thing that was actually burning.

His name's Dale, he's sixty-two. He was a functioning alcoholic for most of my adult life, which is the kind of sentence I used to practice saying for months before I could get through it without my voice shaking.
His liver failed two years ago, and he needed a transplant which took place that October.
After the surgery, he became someone I'd never actually seen before. He was calm, compliant, disciplined. Fourteen medications every morning without complaint. Every blood draw, every follow-up, every PT session. He changed his diet completely. He stopped drinking and never mentioned it like it was hard, even though I know it was.
I used to joke that I'd never seen my dad do anything on time in his life.
I stopped pretty quickly.
The neuropathy started during recovery and was worse than any hangover I'd seen him get through.
The doctors said it was common, that alcohol damages peripheral nerves, and that we needed to give it time.
Time didn't help at all, actually.
By six months post-transplant, my dad was waking up in the middle of the night because his feet felt like they were being burned from the inside. Not tingling, not uncomfortable. Actual burning. The kind that doesn't care what position you're in, doesn't quiet down when you lie still, doesn't care that it's two in the morning and you have a blood draw at eight. He'd just be awake, because sleep wasn't something his body was doing anymore.
He told me once it felt like his feet were having an electrical fire. He said it flat, the way you'd describe the weather.
The showers went around the same time. Water hitting the tops of his feet stung him. He started running it cooler and standing off to one side.
During the day, the numbness was bad enough that he didn't trust his own feet. He started walking slowly and carefully in his own house, like he had to think about each step before he took it. He said his shoes felt like there were bunched up socks in them every time he walked around. Like his feet weren't fully making contact with the fabric of the shoe around it.
He stopped driving at night. Said his feet weren't reliable enough on the pedals. Then the same logic started applying to daytime on bad days, which were most days.
He quit golf eight months after the surgery. He'd gone with the same three guys every Saturday for eleven years. He just stopped showing up, because he couldn't stand for four hours, couldn't feel the cart pedals properly, and couldn't trust his footing on the fairway when the ground wasn't flat. One of the guys called me because he was worried, and I told him Dad was okay.
He was okay. He'd just lost another thing that made him happy.
And here's the part I keep coming back to. He didn't complain about any of it. He'd already given up drinking. Given up his old social life. Gone through a major surgery. And now the nerve pain was taking whatever was left, and he filed all of it under things that were fair consequences for how he'd lived and the choices he made.
Like he'd accepted the terms and wasn't going to argue.
It should've felt endearing, watching him be that determined to get better. It just broke my heart seeing his life get smaller and smaller.
His neurologist put him on gabapentin for the nerve pain.
He took it. Of course he did.
It helped with the burning a little, and it took something else with it.
My dad has always been a talker. He could go forty-five minutes on a bad golf shot or a movie he saw ten years ago. After the gabapentin, he got quieter, shorter, like someone had turned his volume down without mentioning it.
I'd visit and he'd be there in the room, but faint. The best way I can describe it is that he looked like a person who had forgotten, temporarily, that he was supposed to be somewhere.
He spent years checked out because of drinking. He got sober so he could actually be present, for himself and for me. To honor the liver somebody else's family gave him. And then they gave him something for the nerve pain that put him halfway back into that fog. Not the same thing, but close enough that I recognized it. Close enough that it scared me.
He didn't notice, or if he did, he didn't say anything, because complaining wasn't something he was doing anymore. He thought this was what responsible pain management felt like. A trade.
Less pain, less of himself. The burning in his feet cost him sleep. The medication cost him the rest. And he'd accepted both as the terms of a life he felt he'd earned.
That's my dad since the transplant. He follows the instructions and then he makes peace with whatever's left.
His primary care doctor had added a B-complex and a separate B12 capsule to his morning regimen. Both on the approved list. He added them to his lineup and took them every day with the rest of his medication.
They didn't make a difference he could feel. Neither of us thought much about it. The liver was the main thing. Everything else was secondary.
I found the answer on a Sunday afternoon while I was helping him sort his pill case. I do this with him every few weeks because the list changes enough that it needs two sets of eyes.
I started looking up each medication. Not because I thought something was wrong. Just because I wanted to understand what I was handing him.
And then I went back through his hospital paperwork, which I'd read four times and never actually understood.
When they admitted him, they had tested him for a B-vitamin deficiency. Thiamine, B12, folate. They expected to find one. Heavy drinkers usually are depleted, and depletion is the standard explanation for alcohol-related nerve damage. It's the reason the B-complex was on the list in the first place.
His levels came back normal.
Both times.
Nobody had ever explained what that meant. They put him on the vitamins anyway, the way you do, and moved on to the liver.
So I kept reading. And the explanation had been sitting in the medical literature the whole time, and it is not the one anybody had said out loud to us.
Alcohol-related nerve damage isn't primarily a vitamin shortage. It's a poisoning.
Every drink the body processes gets converted into a chemical called acetaldehyde. Not a hangover chemical. A direct nerve toxin. And what acetaldehyde does, specifically, is strip the nerve of something called glutathione.
Glutathione is the nerve's antioxidant shield. It's the one thing standing between the nerve fiber and oxidative damage, and the body has to manufacture it continuously, because it gets used up. Alcohol burns through it faster than the body can rebuild it. Every day. For twenty years.
Then I read the next part and had to read it twice.
The organ that manufactures most of the body's glutathione is the liver.
So the drinking stripped the shield, and the organ responsible for rebuilding the shield was the exact organ the drinking destroyed.
That's the whole picture, and nobody drew it for him. The alcohol stripped the nerve's defenses. The liver that was supposed to replace them had failed. And the supplement they gave him every morning was replacing something he was never short of in the first place.
The nerve wasn't being repaired. It was still burning because the thing that had been burning it never stopped.
He'd stopped drinking, which stopped any more of the poison going in. It did nothing about what was already sitting in the nerve.
Then I found the last piece, and that's the one that actually made me angry.
There is a compound whose job in the human body is regenerating glutathione. It's called alpha lipoic acid. It is not obscure and it is not new. Germany approved it as a prescription treatment for nerve damage in 1966 and has been using it that way ever since. American neurologists prescribe it too — some of them alongside gabapentin, one to quiet the pain and one to go after the damage.
My dad's neurologist had never mentioned it.
But here's the part that would have caught us even if he had.
Alpha lipoic acid comes in two mirror-image forms. R and S. Only the R form occurs in nature, and the R form is the only one used by any biological system on earth. The S form is a manufacturing byproduct. It has no biological function at all.
And nearly every bottle sold in America is a fifty-fifty mix of both.
Which means somebody buying a "600 mg" bottle off the shelf is swallowing 300 mg of the molecule their body actually uses, and 300 mg of factory leftover.
And the nerve formulas that are marketed specifically for this? Most of them run 300 mg of the R form, spread across six enormous pills, buried in a stack of eighteen other ingredients — including the same B vitamins my dad's labs said he didn't need.
Half the studied dose. Six pills. For the one thing that was actually missing.
I sat at his kitchen table for a while after I figured it out. I didn't know how to tell him that he'd been doing everything right and just never been given the full picture.
I found Noverly that same afternoon and spent about an hour reading. 600 mg, which is the dose used in the research, all of it pure R form, in one softgel, suspended in coconut oil so it actually absorbs. No B-vitamin stack. No eighteen ingredients. One thing, at the dose it was studied at, in the form the body can use.
The reviews didn't sound like supplement reviews. They sounded like people writing about my dad.
"I woke up with my feet not on fire and my hands able to make a fist."
"My husband gave up golf. He's back on the course."
I ordered it that night.
It came in a small white pouch with a blue band across the bottom. Thirty cream-colored softgels. One a day, with dinner. No stack, no schedule, no six-pill dose.
He held it and turned it over.
"That's it?"
That's it.
He wasn't skeptical, he was confused. Because his whole life had gotten very complicated since the surgery, and he couldn't figure out where something this small fit into it.
He'd made peace with the burning. With the fog. With Saturday mornings being a thing that used to be the thing he looked forward to.
I told him not to expect anything for a month, and I meant it. Everything honest I'd read said four to twelve weeks, not four days. Nerve is the slowest tissue in the body to change. Anybody promising you faster than that is selling you something worse than what you already have.
Week five, he texted me in the morning. Said he'd slept till six. He hadn't done that since before the surgery.
I didn't make a big deal of it. Neither did he.
It's been five months.
He's not cured. I want to say that clearly, because I remember hating the ads that promised everything when my dad was just trying to get through a single night. He still has neuropathy. He still takes fourteen medications every morning. The liver is the priority and always will be.
But two Saturdays ago I was driving past the golf course and his car was in the parking lot.
I called him that evening. He told me about a shot on the 11th hole he was still annoyed about, and then asked if I wanted to come for dinner.
His voice sounded like his voice.
The same three guys had kept his spot open.
I know not everyone reading this has a dad who drank, or a transplant in the family. Some of you did it on your own. You quit, which is the hardest thing a person can do, and the burning stayed anyway — and somewhere along the way you decided that was the bill, and that you'd earned it.
It isn't a bill. It's a chemical doing what chemicals do, and nobody sat you down and explained the chemistry.
You can't medicate your way out of a chemical burn. Turning the volume down on the signal doesn't do anything to the thing making the noise. The nerve doesn't need to be quieted. It needs its shield back — in the form the body actually uses, at the dose it was actually studied at.
That's what nobody told my dad for two years.
Noverly backs it with a 90-day guarantee. One purchase, no subscription, no autoship, nothing that quietly bills you again next month. I checked, because he's been burned by that before.
You don't have to be certain. You just have to be willing.

Here's what nobody tells you. Almost everything I tried needed me to fail before it could work. The rules reset when I broke them. Naltrexone only worked while I was actively suffering. Dry January was just a countdown to February.

I started to believe I was the problem. Not the drinking. Me. Weak. Undisciplined. One of those people who just can't do it.

Then there was Denise.

Denise runs our benefits program. For years she brought a thermos of "iced tea" to our Friday happy hours that everyone quietly knew wasn't iced tea.

Then, over a few months, she just stopped. Not loudly. No countdown app. No badge. At our holiday happy hour this year she ordered a soda, had half of it, and left early to pick up her kids.

She looked better than anyone in the room.

I watched her leave that soda on the table, still half full, and felt something close to grief.

When I finally asked her how, she said 1 word that made me want to roll my eyes so hard it hurt.

Hypnotherapy.

An app. 15 minutes a night, headphones on. Cheaper than the gin I'd bought that morning.

I'm not a spiritual person. I calculate PTO accrual for a living. My whole personality is a spreadsheet.

So I downloaded Hypnozio for exactly 1 reason. To prove Denise wrong, use it for a week, and ask for my money back.

Week 1, nothing happened. I still poured a glass every night. I almost deleted it.

But I was too tired to keep looking for the next thing. So I kept going.

Then one evening I made tea instead and sat on the terrace, and it wasn't until the kids were in bed that I realized I hadn't thought about the gin once all night.

I didn't fight it. I just forgot to want it.

By week 3, the pull that had run my evenings for 3 years had gone quiet. Not white-knuckled. Not resisted. Quiet.

If you've ever fought a craving you know the difference. Fighting one is loud. It takes up your whole body.

This was just absence.

By month 4 I'd lost 24 of the 30 pounds. My skin came back. I slept through the night for the first time since my youngest was born. Someone at work asked if I'd been away on a retreat.

I started reading about why it worked, and it was the first explanation in 3 years that made sense of my own life.

The part of you that pours the glass at 6 o'clock isn't the part that makes decisions.

It's the part underneath. The one on autopilot.

The same part that drives you all the way home without you consciously choosing a single turn.

That's the part every pill and every countdown and every rule ignores. They talk to the conscious you. They hand you rules.

But the part that pours the glass never got the memo.

Which is exactly why I could follow every rule for 6 days and break on the 7th, alone, in a dark kitchen, hating myself.

It was never that I lacked willpower.

The wiring underneath was just never touched.

A few months ago, my son said something offhand while we were taking out the trash together. He said he used to be able to tell how bad a week was by how heavy the recycling bin got.

He'd known. My kids had known.

For years I thought I was hiding it under that cardboard. I wasn't hiding anything.

That conversation sat with me longer than the one on the terrace did.

It's been 7 months since I've had a drink. Zero.

No pills. No meetings. No white-knuckling a day count.

I sleep through the night. The weight is almost gone. My skin and my hair came back. I call my friends again. I sit on the terrace with tea and actually watch the sunset instead of drinking through it.

When my husband calls from the road now, I remember every conversation.

The cheapest, strangest thing I tried was the only one that worked. Because it was the only one that touched the actual problem.

It was never about the gin.

It was about the wiring underneath.

If you've tried everything and you're still stuck, hear me.

You're not broken. It's not your fault.

You've been fighting the wrong battle this whole time.

Fix the wiring first. Everything else follows.
